article_text:
Jackson Fine Art presents She Was I , a survey of career-defining work by Sam Taylor-Johnson , one of Britain’s most internationally celebrated artists, photographers, and filmmakers. This extensive solo exhibition coincides with the publication of the artist’s major new monograph, Sam Taylor-Johnson: The Self and the Portrait , published by Rizzoli .

The exhibition She Was I traces Taylor-Johnson’s psychologically rich explorations of the self through portraiture in her photography and film work.

Focusing on the self-portraits that are central to Taylor-Johnson’s practice, the selection begins with the early black and white photographs taken in London in the 1990s when she was a student. Then, more than a decade later, the artist returned to self-portraiture with images of herself suspended in her London studio, her body appearing weightless, seemingly held aloft by balloons. In Wired , shot in 2020 in Joshua Tree, Taylor-Johnson now reveals and makes integral to the composition the fragile support mechanisms that elevate her body above the ground in the California desert. Taylor-Johnson’s powerful new series Self Portrait in Dark Water , in which she relies on water to hold her body in otherworldly suspension, will be presented to US audiences for the first time.

The exhibition will also feature a selection of works from the series Crying Men . Created between 2002 and 2004, Taylor-Johnson invited leading male actors to appear before her camera, sat in a moment of intimate reflection, their vulnerability exposed through the act of crying. In parallel to these recognizable individuals, the portraits of the artist’s family and friends captured in the most familial of private settings possess a semi-autobiographical quality.

Seen together, the works in She Was I reveal Taylor-Johnson’s career-long inquiry into the nature of the self and how our individual and complex psyche can be, simultaneously, revealed and concealed.

About the book:

Sam Taylor-Johnson: The Self and the Portrait (Rizzoli, October 6, 2026) is the first comprehensive monograph on the artist, including new writing by Sam Taylor-Johnson alongside texts contributed by Lynsey Addario—award-winning photojournalist and New York Times bestselling author of It’s What I Do —and Tracey Emin, the acclaimed British artist whose work has been exhibited internationally, including at Tate Modern, London; the Musée d’Orsay, Paris; and the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam.

Sam Taylor-Johnson: The Self and the Portrait draws imagery from the artist’s extensive archive. The 224-page volume captures the evolution of her vision from early floating self-portraits through to the quiet intensity of Crying Men and the behind-the-scenes imagery of her cinematic work. The book will be available to purchase at the gallery.

Born in 1967 in London, Taylor-Johnson studied sculpture at Goldsmiths College, emerging alongside the generation of artists who came to prominence in the 1990s and was included in the groundbreaking exhibition Sensation (1997) at the Royal Academy of Arts, London. She turned from sculpture to photography and video early on, merging a cinematic sensibility with the still image. Encouraged toward filmmaking by Anthony Minghella, who produced her Palme d’Or-nominated short Love You More (2008), Taylor-Johnson went on to direct Nowhere Boy (2009), Fifty Shades of Grey (2015), A Million Little Pieces (2018), and Back to Black (2024), earning numerous BAFTA nominations.

Taylor-Johnson’s studio practice has been documented in monographs published by Steidl, including a 2002 volume produced for her Hayward Gallery retrospective and Still Lives (Steidl/BALTIC, 2006). Her editorial and commissioned work ranges from the 2014 series Second Floor , photographing Coco Chanel’s private Paris apartment, to an artist-book edition of F. Scott Fitzgerald’s Tender Is the Night . She won the Illy Café Prize at the 1997 Venice Biennale, was nominated for the Turner Prize in 1998, and was appointed OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) in 2011 for her contributions to British arts and culture.

Taylor-Johnson’s work is held in major public collections including the Museum of Modern Art, New York; the Art Institute of Chicago; the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis; Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum; and National Galleries of Scotland, Edinburgh. She has held solo museum exhibitions at Kunsthalle Zürich (1997), the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebæk (1997), Fondazione Prada, Milan (1998), Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid (2000), Hayward Gallery, London (2002), and BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art, Gateshead (2006). She Was I is Sam Taylor-Johnson’s second solo exhibition with Jackson Fine Art.

Sam Taylor-Johnson : She Was I Exhibition Dates: October 22, 2026 – January 23, 2027 Opening Reception: October 22 | 6-8 PM Jackson Fine Art 3122 East Shadowlawn Ave. NE Atlanta, GA 30305 www.jacksonfineart.com

Opening hours: Tuesday – Saturday, 10AM – 5PM.

article_text:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “ You Can See Everything ,” now playing in theaters.

About halfway through Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” the film’s shock value ratchets up yet again. Even after a full-frontal scene from Holmes’ boyfriend Billy Evans and the convicted fraudster claiming she’s never told a lie, the movie dials it up to 11 with a meta appearance by actress Amanda Seyfried .

Seyfried memorably played the Theranos founder in Hulu’s 2022 series “The Dropout,” which Fielder shows Holmes and Evans for the first time — though it brings the real-life subject to tears. The documentary chronicles the 34 days ahead of Holmes’ 11-year prison sentence, and then Fielder introduces the Seyfried twist halfway through the film after Holmes is incarcerated.

Fielder recruits Seyfried to get her take on some of his odd interactions with Holmes once she’s gone, given that the actress won an Emmy for playing her on “The Dropout.” The meta-ness of Seyfried returning to play Holmes snowballs into her reenacting real-life moments that Fielder and Oppenheim couldn’t capture on camera. Alongside her is “East of Eden” actor Christopher Abbott, who plays Evans, albeit with a smaller role than Seyfried (who goes on to become a main character of the final half).

The two actors recreate a private negotiation between Fielder, Oppenheim and the A24 team that happened before filming for “You Can See Everything” commenced. In it, Seyfried (as Holmes) leaves the conversation to tend to her child, and Abbott (as Evans) demands that he be paid for participating in the documentary. Fielder and Oppenheim (as themselves) push back, arguing that paying the couple would severely discredit the film, but A24 relents and agrees to pay them.

The question then looms over the rest of the film: Did Holmes intentionally leave the room to have deniability on the sketchy payment, or did Evans go rogue and request the money by himself, leaving Holmes out of it? Fielder eventually visits Holmes in prison, where she says she didn’t know about the payment (which we later see recreated in a scene with Seyfried). At the end of the movie, it’s also revealed that Evans dropped his financial request, without further explanation.

In what is perhaps the film’s most meta moment, Seyfried (as Holmes) tells Fielder during their off-camera prison visit, “I don’t want that to happen ever again,” referencing “The Dropout.” In the conversation, Holmes rants about how awful it is that women would “do that” to other women, making a point that Seyfried and the entire “Dropout” team is at fault. She adds that so many of the women incarcerated with her believe that “The Dropout” depicted entirely real events.

Intercut with Seyfried playing Holmes in the prison visit, we see the actress (as herself) reading the script Fielder prepared with his actual conversation from Holmes. Reading Holmes’ accusations, Seyfried’s guard is immediately up. The actress argues that she “didn’t do that to [Holmes]. She did that to herself,” later adding, “it’s not lies. It’s fucking TV.”

Fielder, ever the documentarian, pushes back, questioning whether Seyfried’s scenes in “The Dropout” were completely accurate. Seyfried, still defensive, acknowledges she doesn’t know exactly what happened in Holmes’ life, but that the Theranos founder’s behavior led to assumptions about her, and that’s not Seyfried’s or the show’s fault. This aligns with something Seyfried says earlier in the film: “We’re working in fiction-land” but with “ridiculous amounts of research,” including 10 hours of deposition tapes that she referenced to prepare for her 2022 role.

Earlier in the doc, Seyfried told Fielder she will “reenact whatever you want me to reenact.” Fielder gently reminds her that she’s “not [Holmes],” prompting the actress to ask, “Guess how many people believed I was her when I played her?” She answers with a smile: “A lot.”

Through it all, Seyfried struggles to decipher Holmes. On one hand, she’s empathetic, noting that no woman would want to see another woman in a relationship with someone as manipulative as Evans. But on the other hand, she can’t quite tell whether Holmes is duping everyone — again — creating a push-and-pull between the actress and the imprisoned woman.

Viewers are also left wondering how authentic the film is. Fielder claims Seyfried’s re-created scenes are made using Holmes’ real speech, but we see Fielder develop a warmth toward Holmes. Seyfried questions if Fielder is protecting Holmes by showing a kinder depiction of her with their reenacted scenes. Is Fielder’s kinship with Holmes genuine, or is he playing a heightened version of himself in order to cast doubt on Holmes’ intentions?

The movie ends on a quote from a New York Times interview with Holmes about “The Dropout”: “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” It’s a contentious quote for Holmes, who, throughout the film, asserts that the New York Times misquoted her, who claims she said “a character they created” rather than the attributed “I.” The Times reporter has maintained that the quote is accurate. That single, hotly debated word makes all the difference, and viewers are left to wonder whether the on-camera version of Holmes we see is the real deal or a fictionalized dramatization of the real-life woman.

article_text:
Shashank Walia’s “Birds in the Dark,” about a call center executive whom a police informer mistakes for a suspect, will close the 15th Dharamshala International Film Festival with its India premiere. The festival runs Oct. 29–Nov. 1 at Tibetan Children’s Village in Upper Dharamshala.

Walia’s debut feature took two prizes at the Busan International Film Festival earlier this month.

Related Stories

Ben Frow Stepping Down as Chief Content Officer of 5, Skydance's U.K. Network, After 14 Years

The latest additions to the lineup include “A Fox Under a Pink Moon” by Mehrdad Oskouei. He made the film with Afghan artist Soraya Akhlaghi, and it tracks her attempts to get to her mother in Austria. Paromita Vohra’s “Working Girls” looks at work done by women across India that often goes unseen.

Yashasvi Juyal’s “The Ink Stained Hand and The Missing Thumb,” a South Asia premiere, unfolds at a lonely highway toll booth in northern India, where grief and memory disturb daily routine. Ridham Janve’s “Hunter’s Moon” takes place in the Upper Dhauladhar range.

The shorts section includes the world premiere of Aastha Tiku’s “Dreamboat,” along with Arun Fulara’s “Hudke ki Pyaang Pyaang” and Varun Grover’s “Damned.”

“Curation has always been at the heart of DIFF. While curating, we look for distinctive voices, boundary-pushing filmmaking and films that open up new ways of seeing and thinking. Over the years, this careful and considered approach has allowed DIFF to build a program that is diverse in geography, form and subject, while remaining true to its commitment to independent cinema,” said Bina Paul, the festival’s director of programming.

As previously announced, Rima Das’ “Not a Hero” opens the festival with its South Asia premiere. Titles also include Óliver Laxe’s “Sirāt,” Shaunak Sen’s “Termite,” Gurvinder Singh’s “Rehmat,” Sara Dosa’s “Time and Water,” Dennis Harvey and Lars Lovén’s “Celtic Utopia” and Tanushree Das and Saumyananda Sahi’s “Shadowbox.” “Termite” will have its Asia premiere at the festival and “Rehmat” its India premiere.

Away from the screenings, DIFF’s Himalayan Film Fellows initiative, backed this year by Arthshila, is working with seven filmmakers from the Indian Himalayan Region on their first or second fiction features. Their mentors are Dechen Roder, Umesh Kulkarni and Dominic Sangma. The festival, working with Royal Enfield Social Mission, is also completing 24 community screenings around Kangra this year, at venues that have included schools, nunneries and the district jail.

Filmmakers Ritu Sarin and Tenzing Sonam launched DIFF in 2012.

“When we started DIFF, we wanted to create a space in Dharamshala where independent films could be experienced in a communal setting, and where filmmakers and audiences could spend time with each other beyond the screening room. Fifteen years later, that spirit remains at the heart of the festival. We are excited to welcome everyone back to the mountains for this year’s landmark edition,” said Sarin and Sonam.

The festival runs Oct. 29–Nov. 1 at Tibetan Children’s Village in Upper Dharamshala.

title_original: Aperture Opens at 380 Columbus Avenue
editorial_excerpt_zh: 摄影的新家，自9月18日起向公众开放。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Aperture在哥伦布大道380号开幕", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影的新家，自9月18日起向公众开放", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture剪彩仪式，纽约，2026年9月。摄影：Lloyd McCullough", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture新闻——2026年9月18日", "links": [{"text": "Aperture News", "url": "https://aperture.org/category/aperture-news/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为庆祝Aperture位于纽约上西区的永久新址正式开放，支持者、艺术家和邻里于9月18日上午齐聚剪彩；前一晚则先举办了热闹的庆祝活动。开幕活动为Aperture位于哥伦布大道380号的新篇章举杯。这是一个献给“各地认真投入摄影的摄影师与创意人士”的专属空间，回应了创办者七十四年前的愿景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260918_Aperture_RibbonCutting_0456-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "三十多位艺术家齐聚拍摄合影，以纪念这一重要时刻，也向Aperture的过去与未来致意。到场的其他艺术家包括Emmet Gowin、Richard Renaldi、Sable Elyse Smith、Naima Green、Philip Montgomery、Edward Burtynsky及Carlos Jaramillo。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0860-1024x715.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0744-scaled.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0334-scaled.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0179-scaled.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0499-scaled.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture董事会主席Cathy Kaplan欢迎来宾，并感谢众多资助者与机构的持续支持，使新家得以落成。多位公职人员也到场庆祝Aperture对纽约艺术文化的贡献，包括纽约市议员Gale A. Brewer、纽约州艺术委员会执行主任Erika Mallin、纽约市文化事务局局长Diya Vij、曼哈顿副区长Miesha Smith及纽约州参议员Erik Bottcher。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "剪彩前，Aperture执行主任Sarah Meister表达了深切谢意，并强调哥伦布大道380号的意义：这是一个欢迎人们相聚、交流想法并接触摄影的场所。Meister向支持者、员工和社群致谢时说：“这座美丽的承重砖石建筑中，拱门的每一块砖都需要相邻的砖，才能发挥作用；同样，我们每个人都在促成这个历史时刻的过程中扮演了不可或缺的角色。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260918_Aperture_RibbonCutting_0211.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260918_Aperture_RibbonCutting_0119.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260918_Aperture_RibbonCutting_0115-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "庆祝活动中，来宾预览了书店。这里备有Aperture的新书与经典出版物，也提供与纽约Dashwood Books及新德里Offset Projects合作引入的书籍。来宾还参观了画廊的开幕装置《Aperture Loves New York》：它聚焦植根于Aperture出版历史的艺术家，以照片及相应的Aperture书籍，呈现那些推动摄影媒介发展、捕捉纽约复杂精神的作品。来宾也体验了新的拍照亭，今后访客仍可使用。Aperture如今已向公众开放，并将举办整季艺术家对谈、座谈讨论和新书庆祝活动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture感谢〔原文此处缺少名称〕及Zabar’s对开幕庆祝活动的慷慨支持；香槟由Ruinart提供，葡萄酒由Massican提供。《Aperture Loves New York》的推广支持部分来自纽约市旅游基金会。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture迄今的资本筹募计划，获得了Judy Glickman Lauder、Melissa与James O’Shaughnessy、Vasant Nayak、Thomas R. Schiff、Jon Stryker与Slobodan Randjelović，以及Michael Hoeh和Thompson Family Foundation带来的重大捐赠。Aperture也获得了纽约州艺术委员会及纽约市的重要拨款；市级支持涉及曼哈顿区长、纽约市议会与纽约市文化事务局。这项计划得到Aperture董事会全体参与，以及其他个人和基金会的慷慨支持。新址购置工作由董事会主席Cathy M. Kaplan、董事会房地产委员会主席Helen Nitkin及执行主任Sarah Meister共同领导。融资由非营利社区发展机构LISC NY提供。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Aperture2026-0269_V2-320x256.jpg", "alt": "来源配图", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}]

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Aperture Opens at 380 Columbus Avenue"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The new home for photography, now open to the public as of September 18"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture Ribbon Cutting, New York, September 2026. Photo by Lloyd McCullough"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture News - September 18, 2026", "links": [{"text": "Aperture News", "url": "https://aperture.org/category/aperture-news/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To mark the momentous opening of Aperture’s permanent home in New York’s Upper West Side, supporters, artists, and neighbors gathered for a ceremonial ribbon cutting on the morning of September 18, following festive celebrations the evening before. The opening events toasted Aperture’s new chapter at 380 Columbus Avenue—a dedicated space for “serious photographers and creative people everywhere,” as its founders envisioned seventy-four years ago."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260918_Aperture_RibbonCutting_0456-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Honoring Aperture’s past and future, more than thirty artists gathered to take a group photograph, marking the significance of the occasion. Other artists in attendance included Emmet Gowin, Richard Renaldi, Sable Elyse Smith, Naima Green, Philip Montgomery, Edward Burtynsky, and Carlos Jaramillo."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0860-1024x715.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0744-scaled.jpg", "alt": "Michael Famighetti, Deana Lawson, Hiroshi Sugimoto, Kwame Brathwaite Jr. Photo by Landon Nordeman", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0334-scaled.jpg", "alt": "Rama Duwaji, Sarah Meister. Photo by Landon Nordeman", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0179-scaled.jpg", "alt": "Sarah Meister, Cathy Kaplan, Helen Nitkin. Photo by Landon Nordeman", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260917_Aperture_0499-scaled.jpg", "alt": "Judy Glickman Lauder, Celso Gonzalez-Falla, Elizabeth Kahane, Susan Meiselas, Dawoud Bey. Photo by Landon Nordeman", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Cathy Kaplan, Chair of Aperture’s Board of Trustees, welcomed guests and recognized the many funders and organizations whose steadfast support made the new home possible. Public officials, including New York City Council Member Gale A. Brewer; Erika Mallin, Executive Director of the New York State Council on the Arts; Diya Vij, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs; Miesha Smith, Deputy Borough President for Manhattan; and Erik Bottcher, New York State Senator, joined to celebrate Aperture’s contributions to New York’s arts and culture landscape."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Just before the ribbon-cutting moment, Aperture Executive Director Sarah Meister expressed deep appreciation and emphasized the significance of 380 Columbus Avenue as a welcoming forum to gather, share ideas, and engage with photography. “Just like each brick in the beautiful arches of this load-bearing masonry building needs its neighbor to serve its function, each of us has played an essential role in making this historic moment possible,” said Meister, in thanks to the supporters, staff, and community."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260918_Aperture_RibbonCutting_0211.jpg", "alt": "Cathy Kaplan. Photo by Lloyd McCullough", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260918_Aperture_RibbonCutting_0119.jpg", "alt": "Elizabeth Kahane, Melissa O’Shaughnessy. Photo by Lloyd McCullough", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260918_Aperture_RibbonCutting_0115-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the celebrations, guests previewed the bookstore, stocked with new and classic Aperture publications along with titles in collaboration with Dashwood Books, New York, and Offset Projects, New Delhi, and visited the gallery space featuring the inaugural installation Aperture Loves New York , which showcases artists anchored in Aperture’s publishing history with photographs and corresponding Aperture books that have advanced the medium of photography and captured the complex spirit of New York itself. Guests also stopped by the new photo booth, which will remain available for visitors. Now open to the public, Aperture hosts a full season of artist talks, panel discussions, and book celebrations."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture thanks and Zabar’s for their generous support of the opening celebrations, with champagne provided by Ruinart and wine provided by Massican. Promotional support for Aperture Loves New York is provided in part by the New York City Tourism Foundation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture’s capital campaign to date includes transformative gifts from Judy Glickman Lauder, Melissa and James O’Shaughnessy, Vasant Nayak, Thomas R. Schiff, and Jon Stryker and Slobodan Randjelović, as well as from Michael Hoeh and the Thompson Family Foundation. Aperture received significant grants from New York State Council on the Arts; and City of New York, including the Manhattan Borough President, New York City Council, and New York City Department of Cultural Affairs. article_text:
Aperture Opens at 380 Columbus Avenue

The new home for photography, now open to the public as of September 18

Aperture Ribbon Cutting, New York, September 2026. Photo by Lloyd McCullough

Aperture News - September 18, 2026

To mark the momentous opening of Aperture’s permanent home in New York’s Upper West Side, supporters, artists, and neighbors gathered for a ceremonial ribbon cutting on the morning of September 18, following festive celebrations the evening before. The opening events toasted Aperture’s new chapter at 380 Columbus Avenue—a dedicated space for “serious photographers and creative people everywhere,” as its founders envisioned seventy-four years ago.

Honoring Aperture’s past and future, more than thirty artists gathered to take a group photograph, marking the significance of the occasion. Other artists in attendance included Emmet Gowin, Richard Renaldi, Sable Elyse Smith, Naima Green, Philip Montgomery, Edward Burtynsky, and Carlos Jaramillo.

Cathy Kaplan, Chair of Aperture’s Board of Trustees, welcomed guests and recognized the many funders and organizations whose steadfast support made the new home possible. Public officials, including New York City Council Member Gale A. Brewer; Erika Mallin, Executive Director of the New York State Council on the Arts; Diya Vij, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs; Miesha Smith, Deputy Borough President for Manhattan; and Erik Bottcher, New York State Senator, joined to celebrate Aperture’s contributions to New York’s arts and culture landscape.

Just before the ribbon-cutting moment, Aperture Executive Director Sarah Meister expressed deep appreciation and emphasized the significance of 380 Columbus Avenue as a welcoming forum to gather, share ideas, and engage with photography. “Just like each brick in the beautiful arches of this load-bearing masonry building needs its neighbor to serve its function, each of us has played an essential role in making this historic moment possible,” said Meister, in thanks to the supporters, staff, and community.

At the celebrations, guests previewed the bookstore, stocked with new and classic Aperture publications along with titles in collaboration with Dashwood Books, New York, and Offset Projects, New Delhi, and visited the gallery space featuring the inaugural installation Aperture Loves New York , which showcases artists anchored in Aperture’s publishing history with photographs and corresponding Aperture books that have advanced the medium of photography and captured the complex spirit of New York itself. Guests also stopped by the new photo booth, which will remain available for visitors. Now open to the public, Aperture hosts a full season of artist talks, panel discussions, and book celebrations.

Aperture thanks and Zabar’s for their generous support of the opening celebrations, with champagne provided by Ruinart and wine provided by Massican. Promotional support for Aperture Loves New York is provided in part by the New York City Tourism Foundation.

Aperture’s capital campaign to date includes transformative gifts from Judy Glickman Lauder, Melissa and James O’Shaughnessy, Vasant Nayak, Thomas R. Schiff, and Jon Stryker and Slobodan Randjelović, as well as from Michael Hoeh and the Thompson Family Foundation. Aperture received significant grants from New York State Council on the Arts; and City of New York, including the Manhattan Borough President, New York City Council, and New York City Department of Cultural Affairs. Support for the campaign reflects the full participation of Aperture’s Board of Trustees, along with generous contributions from other individuals and foundations. The acquisition of the new space was led by Cathy M. Kaplan, Chair of Aperture’s Board; Helen Nitkin, Chair of the Board’s Real Estate Committee; and Sarah Meister, Executive Director. Financing has been provided by LISC NY, a nonprofit community development institution.

"因此，毕加索的头脑显得像是一种粘合剂，能够混合并调和平行宇宙、言语流与色彩流、神秘的言语和具有完整意义的笔触，以及对自身和其他艺术家的愿景与持续再创作。这是一项既具理论性又具自传性的艰巨工作，它在感知、想象和现实这一充满生机的物质领域中不断接受考验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "事实上，绘画及其创造性和诗意的动作在画布上不断相遇又不断碰撞，画布是无限的言说与未言、可见与不可见的发生地。它指向一种持续的努力，一种始终如一的张力，旨在从一切规范、一切期望和束缚中获得绝对的解放，以追求一种深刻而绝对的艺术。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“有一次我画了一幅无尽的风景：山丘、露台、大海、树木，我记不清还有什么了。在某个时刻，我在路上遇到了一颗桃子。我带着专注与清晰、带着渴望画下了它。最后我发现，其余的一切我都不在乎了。我只想画那颗水果。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他本想找出那个独一无二的意义宝库——这颗水果。但不可能“在不包含其所有无限客观关系的情况下”直接把它画出来。这就解释了为什么他的艺术能够穿透可言说与可定义的界限，从而永不消逝。它永远在寻找过去和现在的碎片，等待着未来。它始终向前迈进，去寻找无限且不断可更新的联系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一门确实会呼吸的艺术，它不断与他物相连，犹如一棵枝繁叶茂、具有辐射状交织关系的树。就像一种变质的红色，从被毁坏的画布上剥离并“出现在另一块画布上”，就像他人在其他地方说出的言语。就像熟人或陌生人在远距离所经历并相互交流的同一种情感。然而，如果我们在老博物馆的展厅里穿行，接受穿越这些纸页的洗礼，我们将发现毕加索正等在那里，向我们展示他的色彩与言语，引导我们走向不再可怕且不可知的未知。正是他将“横亘在充满敌意的宇宙与我们之间”。这是一个如今越来越不可知、并且需要向导的宇宙。需要像巴勃罗·毕加索这样的人作为向导。", article_text:
Passato e presente. Futuro ed evoluzione. Non sappiamo se il grande Pablo Picasso abbia mai letto le Confessioni di Agostino ma la sua incredibile, drammatica esperienza estetica, prima che esistenziale, testimonia un dato che diventa legge interiore, ferreo comandamento: «Non c’è passato o futuro nell’arte. Se un’opera non può vivere sempre nel presente non deve essere affatto considerata». Una distensio animi estetica, che rivendica un’assolutezza, un’indipendenza, una nettezza per ogni gesto, su ogni tela, per ogni sguardo d’artista.

L’idea del libro Vietato parlare al conducente! Aforismi e pensieri di Pablo Picasso , edito da Abscondita per la collana Carte d’Artisti, di Sandro Montalto – saggista, poeta, drammaturgo ed esperto di aforismi -, ha un’idea alla base estremamente forte. Gettarci, abbandonarci fin dalle prime pagine dinanzi a una sterminata scelta di riflessioni di uno dei più celebri artisti di tutto il mondo tratte da interviste, pubblicazioni e diari di amici e collaboratori stretti ( Zervos, Parmelin, Sabartés, Kahnweiler, Gilot e vari altri).

E scoprire senza mezzi termini che siamo nudi, indifesi dinanzi alla parola, anzi alla pennellata verbale, dura e cruda di Picasso. Nudi come i suoi corpi dipinti ed esposti al mondo. Senza scampo.

Uno zibaldone potente, a metà tra un trattato di estetica, di ontologia e un diario interiore, anche irriverente e indifferente, che ci restituisce un volto inedito e finissimo di Pablo non solo Maestro de pintura ma anche Maître à penser .

La mente di Picasso appare così un mastice in grado miscelare e armonizzare universi paralleli, flussi verbali e flussi di colori, di parole misteriose e pennellate di senso compiuto, di visioni e di continue rielaborazioni su di sé e su altri artisti. Un lavoro teorico e autobiografico allo stesso tempo, assillante, messo costantemente alla prova sul campo della materia viva della percezione, dell’immaginazione e della realtà.

La pittura infatti, il suo gesto creativo e poietico, si incontrano e si scontrano costantemente sulla tela, sede di un infinito detto e non detto, di un visibile e un invisibile. Alla volta di uno sforzo continuo, una costante tensione verso una liberazione assoluta da ogni codice, da ogni aspettativa e vincolo, alla ricerca di un’arte profonda e assoluta.

In fondo Picasso non voleva dipingere «Un nudo dalla testa ai piedi». Voleva soltanto riuscire “a dirlo”. La pittura così, da linguaggio radicale, universale, autocrate e accentratore, diventa un mezzo quasi di salvezza, di riscatto dall’oblio, dalla perdita. Dal moto distruttivo delle cose. Se le persone immortalate nei dipinti da Diego Velázquez erano inevitabilmente diverse dai loro “originali”, a oggi «Non possiamo immaginare Filippo IV in maniera differente da come lui lo ha ritratto». La realtà si rivela allora qualcosa di orrendamente sfuggente e illusorio, persino inesistente: una dimensione che nessun filosofo, artista, storico o scienziato può pretendere di conoscere o dominare.

È dunque, «L’arte è una bugia che ci permette di intuire la verità, per lo meno la verità che ci è dato comprendere». Anzi se l’irruzione della fotografia a cavallo dei secoli XIX e XX libera per Picasso la pittura «Da tutta la letteratura, dagli aneddoti e dal soggetto», sollevandola da ogni missione narrativa, storica e liturgica, tocca proprio alla mano del pittore ricostituire nuovi piani di libertà e nuove forme di poiesis.

Scomparso il soggetto, il centro dello sguardo, la pittura dell’artista può spingersi alla ricerca di dimensioni sempre vive, cangianti, nel tentativo disperante e ossessivo di imitare il flusso, il divenire vivace e implacabile della natura, torcendo le regole della materia, come delle percezioni e delle emozioni.

Così arriva a teorizzare il «Colore che respira», un pigmento in grado di «Raggiungere un punto al di là di se stesso», in una zona neutra dentro la quale poi prevarrà l’altro colore. Un’energia pittorica per l’appunto viva, indipendente, dotata di «Una forza espansiva», che non rimane confinata nei bordi o negli spazi ad essa concessa da qualcuno, tanto meno dal suo creatore. Oppure in grado anche di scovare, cercare particolari, nuclei di senso, simbolici o essenziali, non progettati, non decisi a tavolino.

«Una volta dipinsi un paesaggio interminabile: colline, terrazze, mare, alberi, non so più che cosa. A un certo punto trovai sul mio cammino una pesca. La dipinsi con attenzione ed evidenza, con avidità. Alla fine mi accorsi che di tutto il resto non m’importava nulla. Volevo dipingere proprio quel frutto».

Da dove viene questa pesca? Era di questa realtà, era nella mente del pittore? Sussisteva in entrambe? È un ricordo di vita? È stato un sogno?

Gli sarebbe piaciuto scovare quell’unico scrigno di senso, il frutto. Ma non era possibile dipingerlo direttamente «Senza tutte le sue infinite relazioni oggettive». Questo spiega come la sua arte attraversi i limiti del dicibile e del definibile, per non morire mai. Sempre alla ricerca di frammenti del passato e del presente, in attesa del futuro. Procedendo sempre oltre, alla ricerca di connessioni infinite e sempre rinnovabili.

Un’arte che appunto respira, si lega continuamente ad altro, come un albero ramificato di relazioni e intrecci radiali. Come un rosso metamorfico, tolto da una tela distrutta e «Apparsa in un’altra», come una parola pronunciata da altri in altri luoghi. Come una stessa emozioni che conoscenti o sconosciuti vivono e si scambiano a distanza.

Quando, insieme ad Andrè Derain , Picasso visita il Musée du Trocadéro, viene travolto da un’inedita sensazione di «Muffa e abbandono». Fa per andarsene ma poi comprende che quelle vecchie maschere, quei laceri manufatti sono dei dispositivi, degli strumenti di comunicazione con il sacro e il magico, con ciò che è sconosciuto e pauroso. «Cercavano così di superare il loro terrore attribuendogli una forma e un colore». Ecco, quello che si prova se accettiamo di attraversare queste pagine, come delle vecchie sale di un museo. Troveremo Picasso lì ad aspettarci, a mostrarci i suoi colori e le sue parole, a guidarci verso un ignoto, che non sarà più orrendo e inconoscibile. Sarà lui a «Frapporsi tra l’universo ostile e noi». Un universo oggi sempre più inconoscibile e che necessita di guide. Della guida di uno come Pablo Picasso.

title_original: Global Peace Photo Award: The Hairdryer of Afghan Women in Exile
editorial_title_zh: 全球和平摄影奖：流亡阿富汗女性手中的吹风机
editorial_excerpt_zh: 9月24日星期四，第14届全球和平摄影奖（Global Peace Photo Award）颁奖典礼在奥地利维也纳市政厅举行，并颁发了阿尔弗雷德·弗里德和平奖（Alfred Fried Peace Medals）。在来自144个国家的27,846幅影像中，评审团特别关注了意大利摄影师西尔维娅·阿莱西（Silvia Alessi）的作品，该作品拍摄于……

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "27,846 photographs, 144 countries, and the top prize, worth 6,000 euros, went to a bathroom appliance: the hairdryer. Hairdryers, rather, held aloft at arm’s length by young women who fled Afghanistan. “The Cut” by Silvia Alessi was named Peace Image of the Year 2026 before a packed hall, in the Wappensaal of City Hall, where city councillor Alexandra Rezaei represented the mayor, Michael Ludwig."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "A forbidden trade"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In power since August 2021, the Taliban have also closed beauty salons to women. It was one of the last trades still open to them, and their hair, incidentally, disappears under the headscarf anyway. What their country refuses them, these young exiles now learn in Pakistan, in classrooms equipped with mirrors, hairdressing tools and mannequins."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Juror Peter-Matthias Gaede summed it up in his tribute: every hairdryer becomes a weapon for self-determination, visibility and the right to choose a profession. The word is strong, perhaps too strong for an image whose charm lies in its lightness. Sand, garnet and rust-coloured headscarves stand out against a grey wall, the cables hang like vines, and the half-masked faces look all the more directly at the camera. The symbolism is a little heavy-handed, but the insolence of the raised arms saves it from slogan. The photographer also received the prize for best single image, 1,000 euros provided by the Austrian Photographic Society (PHG)."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/silvia-alessi-the-cut--from-training-to-hidden-practice-1024x682.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "The Cut, From Training to Hidden Practice, Afghanistan © Silvia Alessi", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In an earlier life, Silvia Alessi styled hair for a living. Born in Brescia in 1975, she worked as a hairdresser for over ten years before discovering photojournalism on a trip to Asia in 2004. She has since worked in Japan, India and Iraq, and been published across most major European countries as well as in Israel and the Philippines. Are there more decisive battlegrounds for women’s rights than the hairdressing salon, the school, the university, the doctor’s surgery? No doubt. But what she uncovered there is anything but trivial, she says: these women hold a tool of empowerment in their hands."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Making peace with the sea"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alongside the top prize, three series also received 1,000 euros each. Antonio Denti, born in Catania in 1972, studied anthropology in London before covering Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq, Israel and Gaza for Reuters, then the start of the Arab Spring in Tunisia, natural disasters, contemporary migration and the Pope’s travels. This time he followed, near Rome, African migrant women and their children born in Italy, encouraged to unlearn their fear of water. For them, the Mediterranean remains the memory of a crossing in a makeshift boat, a second desert after the one they had fled."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/1-il-mare-in-mezzo-0001-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Il Mare in Mezzo, Italy © Antonio Denti", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/5-il-mare-in-mezzo-0005-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Il Mare in Mezzo, Italy © Antonio Denti", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I am an intruder into the lives of others,” he says, “and I must at least try, for a few moments, to sense what they themselves are feeling. Photography must be an expression of humanity.” Denti tracked down some of these women years after their crossing, and followed them from their homes to the beach and out into the water, capturing moments of relaxation and daring, but also faces where the fear had not quite lifted. Making peace with the sea is the project, and the series is called “Il Mare in Mezzo” (“The Sea In Between”)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aleksandra Kossowska, 48, based in Warsaw and co-founder of the Poleczki.art centre, travelled to Sebeta, Ethiopia, to photograph blind and visually impaired children in black and white. They live in a spartan shelter, in cramped shared dormitories, far from their families, yet surrounded by care and driven by the desire to achieve independence in the world of the sighted. The photographer scattered clouds of stars over the portraits, then perforated the prints by hand so that the children could touch them too. “The world touches us when we touch it,” she says. Making blindness visible is impossible, she admits herself, and these stars are its translation. One may wonder whether they illuminate or embellish."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/1-the-world-by-touch-1024x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Genzebe Seifu is in the 8th grade. She is 18 years old and came to the school in 2010. She lost her sight suddenly at the age of five when she felt blinded by sunlight and has not been able to see since then. She loves reading books from the school library, especially those about geography, as she aspires to become a geography teacher and travel the world. Her oldest sister lives in Dubai © Aleksandra Kossowska", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/0-title-image-9-the-world-by-touch-1024x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Abebu Besha visits her friend Misra Jemall who underwent a eye surgery a few days earlier. Sebeta, Ethiopia, March 12, 2024 © Aleksandra Kossowska", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Wings among the ruins"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A peace prize for a childhood in Gaza: the pairing is surprising at first. Yet Mahmoud Abu Hamda, 36, a former photography lecturer at the University of Gaza, shows children laughing, a boy playing the violin, swings set up amid the rubble. According to the prize organisers, the photographer was displaced, then injured when the Israeli Air Force bombed a high-rise building, and he documented hunger while starving himself. Perhaps he sought out these carefree moments, he told Magnum, because amid so much misery he too sometimes needed a place to rest. “To breathe.” Magnum has already published his work, which has been shown in Amsterdam, among other places, and won a Lucia Award in 2023."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For the Childrens Peace Image of the Year 2026, the prize went to Sesilia Shainidze, 11, from Batumi, Georgia. Her mother works as an insurance agent, her father as an offshore engineer, and her own camera is currently broken. 27,846 photographs, 144 countries, and the top prize, worth 6,000 euros, went to a bathroom appliance: the hairdryer. Hairdryers, rather, held aloft at arm’s length by young women who fled Afghanistan. “The Cut” by Silvia Alessi was named Peace Image of the Year 2026 before a packed hall, in the Wappensaal of City Hall, where city councillor Alexandra Rezaei represented the mayor, Michael Ludwig.

A forbidden trade

In power since August 2021, the Taliban have also closed beauty salons to women. It was one of the last trades still open to them, and their hair, incidentally, disappears under the headscarf anyway. What their country refuses them, these young exiles now learn in Pakistan, in classrooms equipped with mirrors, hairdressing tools and mannequins.

Juror Peter-Matthias Gaede summed it up in his tribute: every hairdryer becomes a weapon for self-determination, visibility and the right to choose a profession. The word is strong, perhaps too strong for an image whose charm lies in its lightness. Sand, garnet and rust-coloured headscarves stand out against a grey wall, the cables hang like vines, and the half-masked faces look all the more directly at the camera. The symbolism is a little heavy-handed, but the insolence of the raised arms saves it from slogan. The photographer also received the prize for best single image, 1,000 euros provided by the Austrian Photographic Society (PHG).

In an earlier life, Silvia Alessi styled hair for a living. Born in Brescia in 1975, she worked as a hairdresser for over ten years before discovering photojournalism on a trip to Asia in 2004. She has since worked in Japan, India and Iraq, and been published across most major European countries as well as in Israel and the Philippines. Are there more decisive battlegrounds for women’s rights than the hairdressing salon, the school, the university, the doctor’s surgery? No doubt. But what she uncovered there is anything but trivial, she says: these women hold a tool of empowerment in their hands.

Making peace with the sea

Alongside the top prize, three series also received 1,000 euros each. Antonio Denti, born in Catania in 1972, studied anthropology in London before covering Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq, Israel and Gaza for Reuters, then the start of the Arab Spring in Tunisia, natural disasters, contemporary migration and the Pope’s travels. This time he followed, near Rome, African migrant women and their children born in Italy, encouraged to unlearn their fear of water. For them, the Mediterranean remains the memory of a crossing in a makeshift boat, a second desert after the one they had fled.

“I am an intruder into the lives of others,” he says, “and I must at least try, for a few moments, to sense what they themselves are feeling. Photography must be an expression of humanity.” Denti tracked down some of these women years after their crossing, and followed them from their homes to the beach and out into the water, capturing moments of relaxation and daring, but also faces where the fear had not quite lifted. Making peace with the sea is the project, and the series is called “Il Mare in Mezzo” (“The Sea In Between”).

Aleksandra Kossowska, 48, based in Warsaw and co-founder of the Poleczki.art centre, travelled to Sebeta, Ethiopia, to photograph blind and visually impaired children in black and white. They live in a spartan shelter, in cramped shared dormitories, far from their families, yet surrounded by care and driven by the desire to achieve independence in the world of the sighted. The photographer scattered clouds of stars over the portraits, then perforated the prints by hand so that the children could touch them too. “The world touches us when we touch it,” she says. Making blindness visible is impossible, she admits herself, and these stars are its translation. One may wonder whether they illuminate or embellish.

Wings among the ruins

A peace prize for a childhood in Gaza: the pairing is surprising at first. Yet Mahmoud Abu Hamda, 36, a former photography lecturer at the University of Gaza, shows children laughing, a boy playing the violin, swings set up amid the rubble. According to the prize organisers, the photographer was displaced, then injured when the Israeli Air Force bombed a high-rise building, and he documented hunger while starving himself. Perhaps he sought out these carefree moments, he told Magnum, because amid so much misery he too sometimes needed a place to rest. “To breathe.” Magnum has already published his work, which has been shown in Amsterdam, among other places, and won a Lucia Award in 2023.

For the Childrens Peace Image of the Year 2026, the prize went to Sesilia Shainidze, 11, from Batumi, Georgia. Her mother works as an insurance agent, her father as an offshore engineer, and her own camera is currently broken. For “My Family”, she staged a tableau at her grandmother’s house with her grandmother, uncle, aunt, cousins and dog, an idea entirely her own. She also enjoys painting and travelling, and mostly photographs animals, especially her dog, whom she raised herself. She took home 1,000 euros.

Last Thursday, in Vienna, actor Cornelius Obonya, honorary ambassador of UNICEF Austria, delivered the keynote and devoted his speech to the invasion of Ukraine. He closed with a wish: “May the message conveyed in and through your photographs lead to better news from the war-torn regions of this planet.”

One may regret that an awards list surrounded by so many speeches lets the cause speak louder than the writing. But the prize’s initiator, Lois Lammerhuber, had set the frame in his address: “peace is not the absence of war, but something I would describe as a ‘life well lived’.”

The 2026 winners and shortlist are presented on the Global Peace Photo Award website.

article_text:
After more than 20 years in Brazilian film distribution, Alex Levy-Heller’s Rio-based Pipa Pictures is setting up a U.S. base, venturing into co-production as it develops its first two projects with “All Quiet on the Western Front” producer Daniel Dreifuss and Felipe Joffily, best known for his Brazilian box office hit, “Muita calma nessa hora.”

L.A.-based Dreifuss is boarding the fact-based drama “Bloodstained Swan” (“Cisne manchado de sangue”), which Levy-Heller is co-writing and will direct. Joffily will helm road movie “Pan-American Soul” (“Alma Panamericana”) with Brazil’s Downtown Filmes handling distribution.

Related Stories

Byron Allen Earns Profit After Selling All the Starz Stock He Bought From Steven Mnuchin

Starz Beats Wall Street's Q3 Earnings Estimates as Net Loss Narrows to $35 Million, Linear TV Revenue Dips

“Our goal is to connect Brazilian producers with American producers to develop projects and build international partnerships, mainly between Brazil and the United States, but also with other countries. We want to serve as a bridge between these producers, helping them work together on international co-productions, while also expanding the reach of Brazilian films through our distribution catalog,” Levy-Heller told Variety.

The move comes as interest in Brazilian films has spiked given the recent back-to-back success of two films at the Oscars : 2025 Best International Feature winner “I’m Still Here” and in 2026, Kleber Mendonça Filho’s political drama “The Secret Agent,” which scored four nominations including for lead Wagner Moura.

The Pipa Pictures CEO will be attending the American Film Market ( AFM ), now underway until Nov. 15.

A historical thriller inspired by actual events, “Bloodstained Swan” (working title) will be produced by Brazil’s Alelo Filmes and Dreifuss’s Anima Pictures, with Pipa Pictures co-producing.

Set in the 1960s, the story spans Rio de Janeiro, Goiás, São Paulo and Montevideo as it follows Herbert Cukurs, a Latvian immigrant who introduced the popular swan-shaped pedal boats to the Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon in Rio. All went well for him until he was identified by a Holocaust survivor as the notorious Butcher of Riga, the Latvian aviator who became a Nazi collaborator and Holocaust perpetrator during World War II.

As the story blends psychological suspense and espionage, it also addresses the flight of Nazis to Latin America and the Mossad operations to track them down.

“One of my objectives as a filmmaker is to make films that are both Brazilian and Jewish because that’s something that we don’t have much of in Brazil,” said Levy-Heller, who expects Dreifuss to bring his own creative vision to the project, along with valuable talent and expertise in script development and producing.

“Incidentally, Dreifuss and I are both descendants of Holocaust survivors,” he added.

“I think the story is fascinating. It’s one of those stories I’m always drawn to because it sounds implausible, almost hard to believe it’s true. Most people in Rio, or those who have visited, have seen the swan-shaped paddle boats. I don’t think anyone looking at that romantic, playful, nostalgic image would imagine that the person behind it was a Nazi who fled and reinvented himself with a new life. It’s such a contradiction to the person he was, a wolf in sheep’s clothing,” said Dreifuss.

“I’m excited by the challenge of bringing such an ambitious narrative to life as an international co-production, potentially involving Uruguay and Germany. Drawing on my experience working across different cultures, territories and funding systems, I hope to help make the project a reality,” he told Variety, adding that while this project serves as Levy-Heller’s expansion into the U.S., he’s on a “reverse route,” returning to produce again in Brazil with Brazilian stories.

The second co-production, “Pan-American Soul,” is produced by Fiti Produções and Pipa Pictures in the U.S. It is based on the actual adventures of former surfing magazine editor Adrian Kojin as he drove across the Americas on a motorcycle with a surfboard strapped to his back.

Fiti Produções head Carlos Sanfelice brings his experience in surfing documentaries.

“We chose Joffily to direct as he’s capable of directing both mainstream and auteur films,” said Levy-Heller, who added: “He also likes to surf!”

Kojin rode across the Americas in the 1980s, when several countries were experiencing political turmoil, placing the story against the political backdrop of the time. “At the same time, it is a journey of self-discovery, as he gains new perspectives and insights along the way.”

“I think it’s a great story for an international co-production so that’s where Pipa Pictures comes in.

Pipa Pictures has handled the release of more than 50 feature films, both fiction and documentary. Its catalog spans a range of genres and production profiles, from independent and auteur cinema to titles with broader mainstream appeal.

Among the films it has distributed are “Elvis & Madonna,” “Jovens Polacas,” “Noites de Alface,” “Lima Barreto” and “Licença para Enlouquecer.” It has partnered on projects with Globo Filmes, Globoplay, Telecine, Turner and Canal Brasil.

For the first half of 2027, Pipa Pictures is preparing the releases of “Revoada – Versão Steampunk,” an animated film by Ducca Rios produced by Origem Content; “Malick,” by Cassio Tolpolar and Modou Awa Dieye, selected for the Novos Rumos competition at the Rio Film Festival; and “O Mundo Que Eu Conheço Lá Não Existe Mais,” by Tiago Luciano, produced by Luc Filmes and starring Lucy Ramos and Eduardo Moscovis.

Quel a été votre parcours avant de devenir producteur de films ?

Pendant mes études d’ingénieur, quelqu’un qui travaillait à l’INA [ Institut national de l’audiovisuel, ndlr ] m’a parlé d’une petite unité d’une quarantaine de personnes qui s’appelait le Département des programmes de création et de recherche et avait pour mission de découvrir de nouveaux auteurs et de nouvelles formes d’écriture. J’y ai travaillé cinq ans et j’y ai rencontré les frères Dardenne et plein de cinéastes avec qui j’allais travailler plus tard comme Nicolas Philibert, Chantal Akerman, Jean-Louis Comolli. C’était un lieu de très grande liberté qui a généré les essais vidéo de Jean-Luc Godard, les films de Raoul Ruiz et de Jean Eustache. Même si je n’étais pas directement producteur et m’occupais plutôt d’organisation générale, cette aventure créative a formé mon goût.

Jean-Pierre et Luc Dardenne : « On a toujours le désir de filmer comme si c’était la première fois que ce que nous filmons apparaît. »

C’est suite à cette expérience que vous avez créé les sociétés de production Archipel 33 et Archipel 35 ?

Après l’INA, je rejoins un ami qui venait de créer sa société, Initial Groupe. On a produit Le Miraculé de Jean-Pierre Mocky ou Les Jeux de société d’Éric Rohmer. Et en 1988, je crée une première structure pour la télévision, Archipel 33, où je produis des documentaires puis des fictions, comme Les Derniers jours d’Emmanuel Kant de Philippe Collin. En 1997, je crée Archipel 35, pour des longs métrages de cinéma, et je commence avec Saint-Cyr ( sorti en 2000, ndlr ) de Patricia Mazuy , avec Isabelle Huppert. Une de mes collaboratrices avait lu La Maison d’Esther , livre d’Yves Dangerfield qui raconte la création de l’école de Saint-Cyr par Madame de Maintenon, et j’ai cherché pour l’adaptation quelqu’un qui puisse apporter un regard personnel et dynamiter le genre du film en costumes. J’avais été impressionné par Peaux de vaches [ premier long métrage de Patricia Mazuy, sorti en 1989, ndlr ] et j’ai donc approché Patricia Mazuy. On s’est lancés dans la production du film, qui m’a bien secoué !

L’idée d’Archipel 35 était donc d’emblée de produire des films ambitieux artistiquement ?

C’était mon héritage de l’INA. J’étais dans un cinéma quand même atypique, avec l’envie d’avoir un regard d’auteur affirmé sur la façon de traiter la narration, la forme. Le Fils, des frères Dardenne, est le film qui a suivi Saint-Cyr et qui m’a un peu sauvé car j’étais mal financièrement. Quand j’avais connu les Dardenne à l’INA à la fin des années 1970, je n’étais pas encore vraiment producteur et Jean-Pierre et Luc n’étaient pas encore vraiment cinéastes – l’un était assistant opérateur et l’autre assistant réalisateur. Nos chemins s’étaient croisés durant les vingt années suivantes car ils avaient réalisé beaucoup de documentaires avant de passer à la fiction et on avait ça en commun. En 2000, alors que les Dardenne venaient d’avoir la Palme d’or pour Rosetta , Luc me dit que ce serait bien qu’on travaille ensemble et il m’envoie le scénario du Fils. Cela a été le début d’une longue et heureuse aventure puisqu’on a fait neuf films ensemble et que tous ont été en compétition à Cannes. Et même si je n’aurai plus de société de production, car Archipel 35 appartient désormais à mk2, je serai à nouveau coproducteur pour la France du prochain film des Dardenne [ prévu pour être tourné l’année prochaine, ndlr] par l’intermédiaire de Diaphana.

Vous avez aussi produit Bamako d’Abderrahmane Sissako, qui avait la particularité d’être une production franco-américano-malienne. Avec Danny Glover, acteur américain vu notamment dans L’Arme fatale , comme producteur associé.

Au départ, le film était pour Arte et la télévision. Danny Glover a lui été amené dans le financement par Abderrahmane Sissako, qui le connaissait et lui a aussi confié dans le film un rôle de cow-boy. L’aventure a été extraordinaire : se retrouver au Mali dans cette cour avec tous ces avocats était très joyeux [Bamako imagine un procès intenté au FMI et à la Banque mondiale par la société civile africaine et fait jouer de vrais avocats, ndlr] . Quand on a vu le film, on s’est dit qu’on pouvait peut-être sortir du seul circuit de télévision. Il a été sélectionné hors compétition à Cannes en 2006, avec un accueil formidable, et j’ai discuté avec Arte de la possibilité de le sortir en salles. On l’a retransformé en film de cinéma et il a fait plus de 200 000 entrées en France.

Parmi vos productions mémorables, il y a L’Exercice de l’État de Pierre Schoeller, sorti en 2011. L’idée était là encore de bousculer les codes ?

En fait, je choisis les cinéastes avant de choisir les projets. Pierre Schoeller avait réalisé Zéro défaut | présenté en 2003 à l’ACID à Cannes, ndlr] et je lui ai dit que je voulais travailler avec lui. Il m’a parlé de son désir de faire un film politique sur la notion de service de l’État. Mais il est ensuite passé à autre chose et a écrit le scénario de Versailles. Je lui ai avoué que je ne serais peut-être pas le bon producteur pour ce film, qu’il a donc fait sans moi. Mais après Versailles, il me rappelle car il avait enfin trouvé la forme de son film politique. Ce sont parfois de longs processus. Et L’Exercice de l’État a clairement marqué le genre du cinéma politique. Olivier Gourmet [ qui joue dans L’Exercice de l’État un ministre français des Transports confrontés à diverses crises, ndlr] est d’ailleurs l’acteur avec lequel j’ai le plus travaillé, entre les films des frères Dardenne, Home d’Ursula Meier ou le cinéma de Pierre Schoeller.

Oui car vous avez aussi produit le film suivant de Pierre Schoeller, Un peuple et son roi …

Pierre voulait depuis longtemps réaliser un film sur la Révolution française. Et cela a pris huit ans. Le projet était de faire un film en deux parties : Pierre a écrit le premier volet [ qui va de la prise de la Bastille du 14 juillet 1789 à l’exécution de Louis XVI en janvier 1793, ndlr ] et le deuxième volet commençait après l’exécution du roi et allait jusqu’à la fin de Thermidor en juillet 1794. On a chiffré le scénario de la première partie à 21 millions d’euros, mais on s’est vite aperçus qu’avec toutes les coproductions possibles mises bout à bout on réunissait seulement 15 millions. Pierre a dû couper dans le scénario et ce n’était pas simple car il y a trois niveaux de récit : l’atelier du verrier avec Olivier Gourmet, la cour de Louis XVI joué par Laurent Lafitte et l’Assemblée nationale [ avec Louis Garrel en Robespierre, ndlr]. Et il y a en plus des histoires intimes comme la relation entre Gaspard Ulliel et Adèle Haenel. Le film avait un côté visionnaire mais le premier coup sur la tête fut de ne pas être sélectionné en compétition à Cannes, alors que tout le monde s’y attendait. Un peuple et son roi a finalement été montré à Venise hors compétition et a fait 320 000 entrées en France, ce qui n’était pas suffisant pour faire une suite. Cela a été douloureux, mais c’est un film que j’aime beaucoup. Je pense qu’il va durer et il est souvent demandé pour des projections à l’étranger.

Entretemps, vous aviez produit Bird People, sorti en 2014, qui reste le dernier film en date de Pascale Ferran…

J’avais très envie de travailler avec Pascale Ferran, dont j’adore Petits arrangements avec les morts et Lady Chatterley . Elle m’a parlé de Bird People et c’était un vrai pari [ le film suit une femme de chambre, jouée par Anaïs Demoustier, qui se transforme en moineau, ndlr ]. On est parfois devenus fous avec ces moineaux… Pascale est passionnée par les questions de rapport avec le vivant et de communication entre le monde humain et le monde animal et elle avait trouvé une manière de travailler avec les moineaux : elle leur avait donné des prénoms et savait exactement quel moineau elle souhaitait pour telle ou telle prise. On était bluffés de voir les oiseaux faire ce qu’elle voulait ! Pascale n’a malheureusement plus refait de film depuis Bird People, oui. Elle a été très investie dans La Cinetek et les César, mais j’espère qu’elle reviendra un jour au cinéma.

De votre côté, vous arrêtez donc vos activités au sein d’ Archipel 35 et avez choisi de transmettre votre catalogue de films à mk2. Qu’est-ce qui a guidé ce choix ?

J’ai vu les différents types de transmission de films qui peuvent exister et j’ai vu qu’il y avait parfois des films dont les droits se retrouvent bloqués, comme ce fut le cas pour La Maman et la Putain . Selon moi, la détention individuelle des droits d’un film n’est pas forcément la solution, donc je me suis dit qu’il ne fallait pas m’y prendre trop tard pour transmettre et qu’il fallait anticiper. Et mk2 est extrêmement bien organisé pour la gestion des catalogues et réfléchit à la façon dont on peut aujourd’hui faire vivre des œuvres de patrimoine, trouver des nouveaux modes d’exploitation, toucher de jeunes publics.

Ils ont ainsi créé mk2 alt , une alternative pour la distribution dans des circuits particuliers et ont mis au point une plateforme permettant de gérer les demandes de festivals, de salles indépendantes ou d’associations qui voudraient faire une projection unique. C’est important pour les cinéastes car il s’agit de la qualité des regards plus que de rentabilité. Vingt ans après avoir fait un film, vous pouvez avoir une projection avec un public intéressé et un débat.

De façon plus globale, comment voyez-vous l’avenir du cinéma et les menaces qui pèsent parfois sur lui ?

Ma conviction est que pour continuer à faire vivre les œuvres, il faut continuer à faire vivre les salles de cinéma. Le jour où il n’y aura plus de salles, mêmes si les œuvres sont conservées et accessibles sur des plateformes, quelque chose sera perdu dans le rapport au cinéma et dans ce sentiment d’émotions collectives partagées. On a en France la chance exceptionnelle d’avoir un parc de salles formidable. La base c’est que les films soient conservés. Je suis d’accord avec ce que disait Henri Langlois ( pionnier de la conservation des films et cofondateur de la Cinémathèque française en 1936, ndlr ) : « Il faut tout garder ».

Parce qu’on ne sait pas ce qu’il peut se passer autour d’une œuvre. On a parfois l’impression que certains films vieillissent et meurent puis tout d’un coup ils ressuscitent. Il faut garder cette possibilité ouverte de redécouvrir un film. Je pense qu’il y a aussi une appétence des jeunes générations pour le cinéma de patrimoine et pour la circulation et la continuité de l’histoire du cinéma. Quand je me suis construit une cinéphilie dans les années 1970, il y avait quand même moins de films qu’aujourd’hui, où l’on peut se perdre dans une masse incroyable. Il faut éditorialiser et guider, comme j’ai moi pu être guidé dans ma jeunesse par des ciné-clubs ou des émissions de cinéma à la télévision qui aujourd’hui existent moins.

article_text:
BAFTA trustees may have violated U.K. charity and company laws by accepting complimentary awards show tickets that were not disclosed in the organization’s financial accounts, according to allegations raised at the British Academy’s annual general meeting this week.

Michael Pritchett, chair of BAFTA’s membership council, said legal advice he commissioned suggested that trustees who approved the organization’s accounts may have committed offenses under the Charities Act and Companies Act, The Guardian reported Wednesday.

Fox's $22 Billion Roku Deal Approved by Shareholders of Both Companies

The British Academy of Film and Television Arts, which operates as a registered charity, previously allowed trustees to bring guests to its ceremonies, a practice that is said to have been in place for as long as two decades. The complimentary seats reportedly included premium tickets to the BAFTA Film Awards valued at up to £2,000 ($2,660).

Pritchett raised the concerns at BAFTA’s annual general meeting on Monday, arguing that the ticket arrangements conflicted with the organization’s governing rules, which prohibit trustees from receiving remuneration or other benefits from the charity.

The allegations also raise questions about BAFTA’s financial disclosures. The organization’s 2024 and 2025 accounts stated that trustees received no remuneration for their services, while its public register reported no payments or benefits.

According to Pritchett, the legal advice suggested that trustees who approved those accounts may have violated their obligations under U.K. law. He also questioned whether the complimentary tickets should have been subject to taxes dating back to 2016, potentially leaving BAFTA liable for unpaid National Insurance contributions.

Pritchett called for trustees to repay any money owed, settle outstanding taxes and correct the organization’s financial accounts if necessary. He also criticized a senior BAFTA executive for declining to provide records identifying which trustees had received a complimentary ticket.

BAFTA discontinued its longstanding guest-ticket policy in 2025 following a recommendation from its governance committee. The organization has since launched an independent review into the long-running arrangement.

BAFTA’s outgoing chair, Sara Putt, said the organization had already taken the steps to address the concerns and noted that Pritchett’s legal advice was based on limited information, while BAFTA’s own legal advisers had access to a more complete account of the circumstances.

“Trustees of BAFTA are invited to attend events in a working capacity, representing the Academy in an ambassadorial role, and prior to 2025 they could also bring a ‘plus one’ guest to accompany them,” a BAFTA spokesperson told Variety . “In 2025 BAFTA decided to review its guest tickets arrangements and discontinued the long-standing custom and practice of trustees inviting a plus one. The Board has since established an independent review group to consider the historic guest ticket arrangement – the review is underway.”

No legal violations have been formally established.

article_text:
Endlessly curious, irreverent, ingenious, easily bored. It’s hard not to think of Carson as a Laureate for our times, writes Ella Frears

The poets are ecstatic. Canadian writer, translator, essayist and beloved poet-of-poets Anne Carson has been awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature. At the prize announcement on 8 October the secretary of the Swedish Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, said that she’d spoken to Carson on the phone to inform her of the award and that Carson ‘had time to tell me… that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind’. If you think that’s pretentious, I’m here to explain why it’s not. Or at least why she’s earned the right to be.

One of the most impressive things about Anne Carson is the consistency and diversity of her output. Since Eros the Bittersweet in 1986, a reworking of her doctoral thesis, Carson has published over 20 books of poetry, essays, translations and other writings. Every book takes a different form than the last; each is startlingly good on its own terms – experimental, audacious books that blend modern language and ideas with intricate intertextuality. When asked what motivates her formal shifting in an interview , Carson said: ‘Boredom, I guess.’

Carson started as a translator and a teacher of classics, a lifelong passion that started when a high school Latin teacher offered her extra lessons in Ancient Greek during lunchbreaks. One of her most famous works is If Not, Winter (2002) – her translations of the Ancient Greek poet Sappho, a queer musical genius whose works on life, desire, exile and shame survive only in fragments. Carson chooses to represent what is missing, and therefore unsaid (or unheard), with square brackets. At times we get a good chunk of Sappho’s songs, others we must decide how we read them, what we can feel or intuit in the gaps. ‘Fragment 38’ just reads, ‘you burn me’ – three words that get both sexier and more profound with each reading.

Carson’s sustained interest has been in female figures, especially those who represent some element of high femininity, sexuality or beauty. Her works have explored Antigone, Emily Brontë, Brigitte Bardot and Helen of Troy, whom she conflates with Marilyn Monroe in her play Norma Jeane Baker of Troy (2019). She’s interested in their humour, what they chose to say, the push and pull of their femininity – how much of a mask it is, how much of a choice or burden. She is less concerned with ‘truth’ or linear time. In her translation of Antigone, Antigonick (2012), she has the two sisters discussing the German philosopher Hegel.

Then there’s Short Talks (1992), a book of small, blocky prose poems, each presenting itself as a micro lecture on something – hedonism, reading, trout, Ovid, rain, the sensation of airplane takeoff, and so on. In ‘Short Talk on Major and Minor’ she begins,

Major things are wind, evil, a good fighting horse, prepositions, inexhaustible love, the way people choose their king.

There is little more linguistically satisfying than a good list. It’s something Carson is particularly brilliant at. In ‘God’s List of Liquids’, from her 1995 book Glass, Irony & God , there’s another:

For I made their flesh as a sieve

wrote God at the top of the page and then listed in order: Alcohol Blood Gratitude Memory Semen Song Tears Time.

Beyond structural or thematic transformation, Carson has also experimented with the physicality of the book itself. Nox (2010) is part fragmentary elegy or ‘epitaph’ for her brother, who was absent for most of her life, and part translation of a poem by the Roman poet Catullus. It takes the form of one long concertina booklet in a box containing photographs, collages, text works and ephemera to devastating effect. Float (2016) gathers 22 separate chapbooks that can be rearranged and read in any order. Indeed, there is a lot of overlap in Carson’s work between visual art and poetry – and she has proved influential to contemporary artists Roni Horn, Tacita Dean , Johanna Hedva and more; in many ways, poetry, in its consideration of space, shape and image, is closer to art than it is to prose. Of course, poems by artists, and art by poets, is often bad. Both parties seem to fail to understand what makes the other work and lack the dedication to learn it. Which makes Carson’s successful cross into visual art all the more impressive: she knows when to take things seriously; when not to. It’s also because she’s, well, cool. Carson is seventy-six, has a bob, glasses, often dressed in baggy suit and tie – think chic disgruntled geography teacher.

While somewhat allergic to being a public figure onstage, there have been many iconic moments discussed and shared. In 2025 she delivered one of the annual LRB lectures wearing boxing gloves – a reference to the boxing class she’s been taking since and because of her Parkinson’s diagnosis. She is a deadpanning master and infinitely quotable. Red Doc> , the 2013 sequel to her much-lauded Autobiography of Red (1998), is so titled because that’s what it automatically saved as on her computer. ‘If prose is a house,’ she said in an interview, ‘poetry is a man on fire running quite fast through it.’ She can be withering in an audience Q&A, or with those chairing her in conversations – which, depending on how you are with schadenfreude, is either excruciating or thrilling (in fact, her command of the camera , and inadvertently of the many adoring online, marks her out as one of the rare laureates for these times in particular). Her texts are irony-soaked and frequently silly, but always with a scholarly intensity. Whatever she is writing about, be it Hegel, Keats, volcanoes or Rosalía , she turns her intelligence towards it like a searchlight, full-beam.

In 2013 I sat at the back of a packed London bookshop to see her read from Red Doc>. While marvelling at the genius of the writing, it also occurred to me that I’d never heard anyone say the word ‘dick’ better than she did. Thirteen years and one Nobel Prize later, this is still part of the magic of her writing. There is no such thing as highbrow or lowbrow in Carson’s oeuvre – there is only interest and language; boredom and brilliance.

article_text:
I f I’d ever wanted children, the films showing at the 59th edition of the International Fantastic film festival of Catalonia in the coastal town of Sitges, south of Barcelona, would have soon set me straight. This year’s recurring themes were explosive parturition, chewed-up nipples and the fruit of the womb turning out to be at best sociopathic, at worst inhuman.

The theme was celebrated in an evil-kiddy exhibition at the Miramar Cultural Centre, marking the 50th anniversary of Narciso Ibáñez Serrador’s “fantaterror” classic Who Can Kill a Child? , some of which was filmed in Sitges itself. The expo traced the subgenre from 1956’s The Bad Seed, via Rosemary’s Baby and The Exorcist, to this year’s Nightborn , in which poor Rupert Grint, as the hapless husband, is no match for the developing folk-horror bond between his depressed wife, their newborn “child”, and the spooky forest surrounding their house. Finnish director Hanna Bergholm, in her introduction, confessed it was inspired by her experiences of motherhood. Only up to a point, one hopes.

Postpartum depression reared its head again in Mutter: The Diary of a Mother from Turkish director Alphan Eşeli, which begins with a father taking one look at his newborn offspring and fleeing into the woods. Hazar Ergüçlü’s terrific central performance keeps the focus on the social and economic plight of being a single parent, even when your baby resembles the one in Eraserhead.

As usual, a third of the titles in competition here were directed by women. Indeed, winner of this year’s best feature film award was Marion Le Coroller’s Sanguine (AKA Species), which followed in the gloopy French body horror footsteps of Julia Ducournau (Raw) and Coralie Fargeat (The Substance) with a medical intern developing a disfiguring skin condition that will have anyone who ever squeezed a pimple squirming in sympathy. The festival’s award for best female performance went to Jasmine Trinca as a mother who enters into a diabolical pact in Paolo Strippoli’s indecently entertaining The Spiral, though it is supporting actor Valeria Bruni Tedeschi who steals all her scenes as a soigné Mephistopheles in a trenchcoat.

Meanwhile, best actor went to Benoît Magimel, oozing menace in one of his sleazy white suits in Léa Mysius’s The Birthday Party, a finely wrought home invasion thriller, and another of the films pivoting on a fraught mother-child relationship. It was heartening to see so many female protagonists in genre films, even ones by male directors such as Casey Affleck, whose Company , with its Russian doll structure, slowly morphs from a frontier western into a spine-tingling tale of the supernatural.

Elsewhere, young women train as mermaids (Titanic Ocean, which teases the possibility of a mermaid-shark face-off, but fails to deliver), or bond with their abductors (The Daughters), or face off against a sociopathic youngster who infiltrates her snowed-in scout troop (11).

Alas, I was so busy watching these that I missed the 4K restoration of Jimmy Wang Yu’s Master of the Flying Guillotine from 1976 with its glorious krautrock soundtrack. But I did get to pay my respects to the late, great Sam Neill, who provided the voice of a magpie in Dario Russo’s bawdy, unabashedly full-frontal Australian folk yarn The Fox . The stacked cast includes Jai Courtney and Olivia Colman as the voice of a wily talking fox.

My favourite films of the festival included Javier Ruiz Caldera’s 5 More Minutes, which manages to put a new spin on the time-loop subgenre, its early lighthearted tone sliding into darker Timecrimes territory. Then there was The Mouths, about a cursed tree, a return to J-horror form from Takashi Shimizu (The Grudge) that gets more sinister and disorientating as it goes on, plus Sabu’s Taiwanese-Japanese co-production Arrested Memory, in which a traumatised Taipei cop suffering from Guy-Pearce-in-Memento syndrome bumbles his way through kidnapping, drug deals and car chases, to deadpan but ultimately hilarious effect. But best of all was Joko Anwar’s Ghost in the Cell, in which all the usual prison tropes – rioting, brutal guards, shivs, the threat of sexual violence – are supplemented by a supernatural curse, arty splatter, interpretative dance, a commentary on Indonesian corruption, and – best of all – an unexpectedly warmhearted vibe. Fortunately for everyone, it has a UK release on digital platforms from 26 October .
