article_text:
H irokazu Kore-eda’s sad and beautiful film is about friendship, about the ecstasy and burden of success and about what it means to have an artistic vocation, especially when that vocation is pursued collaboratively, with your best friend. It is adapted by Kore-eda from the standalone, or “one-shot”, online manga story of the same title by Tatsuki Fujimoto, which has in fact already had an anime movie adaptation.

Fujino, played by Furi Nanase as a 13-year-old and later by Natsuki Deguchi, is a dedicated would-be manga artist who dreams of being published and adapted for the movies. It is her personal and artistic destiny to come into contact, in her early teens, with fellow manga obsessive Kyomoto, who is played first by Rokka Okada and then as an adult by Aju Makita. Theirs is a kind of platonic but passionate love story.

Fujino begins the story as someone who is very pleased with herself. In school, she has became a virtual celebrity for her simple four-frame yonkoma manga strips in the class magazine. But then her homeroom teacher tells her that he is giving space to a regular manga from another girl, Kyomoto, who suffers from anxiety and never comes into school. Kyomoto’s work stuns Fujino. It seems to her (and all her classmates) to be patently better than hers. Her own work had been simplistically about the faces and the dialogue and the story; Kyomoto’s is more subtly about background ambience – the still life-type landscapes and scenes are far more accomplished.

Fujino feels like a Mozart who suddenly turned into a Salieri. She more or less abandons manga in that moment, morosely pursuing sports, in particular karate. When, at the end of term, her teacher asks her to drop off Kyomoto’s graduation certificate at her house – Kore-era playfully allows us to see that the teacher is trying to engineer a friendship between these two young people – Fujino is resentful and reluctant. She goes there intending brusquely to leave the item and go, but a chaotic mishap means they meet face to face and Kyomoto emotionally calls her “sensei” and says she is her biggest fan. Fujino joyfully resumes drawing and they become soulmates and partners, fusing into one manga creator, an ideal team, winning prizes and commissions. Fujino devises the foregrounded story and characters while Kyomoto’s considered artistry creates the deep emotional mood and context.

But just when they are on a roll, their careers at a staggering momentum that other, older, artists can only dream of … Kyomoto says she wants to quit and go to art college, to be a better artist, while she still has enough time, enough humility to learn. Fujino is furious and the break between them is more painful, more important, than any sundered love affair.

Kore-eda shows us the heartbreak that this leads to, and to an agonising “sliding doors” type reverie about how things could have been different, how Fujino could have redeemed herself as the lesser artist. Fujino wants to reach into the past and change things: and in a sense that is what artists do, especially those whose work is strongly personal or autobiographical. They look back, they retrace their steps to the wellspring of their inspiration, the source of their life’s meaning; they see the form and substance of experiences whose meaning they could not grasp at the time.

Or perhaps it is that they create the form and substance and impose it retrospectively. Looking back is an authentic, vital gesture, but outside the realm of art it is poignant and futile. You can change nothing by looking back; it is simply a forum for sadness and regret. Such is the emotional dynamic of this engrossing, affecting film from Kore-eda, a film of great clarity, intimacy and high seriousness.

article_text:
On the rue Dieu, a few steps from the Canal Saint-Martin, stands the Maison agnès b.: the brand’s international headquarters, and the historic atelier where pattern makers and seamstresses work up the prototypes on a vast open floor the house calls the beehive. The place is normally closed to the public. It opens, exceptionally, for the festival, which floods Paris and the Île-de-France for the whole month of November and has named the designer godmother of its seventh edition.

The selection is agnès b.’s own. She proposed the subject herself to Emmanuelle de l’Ecotais, the festival’s director. “When I arrived, she had laid out all her photographs on a big table. She said to me: ‘I wanted to show you this,’” recalls the founder of Photo Days. Shown once in Marseille in the early 2000s, the prints had since vanished from view. The two women agreed on the spot.

The story goes back to 1987. That year, the fashion magazine Elle sent the designer to Moscow, then the capital of the Soviet Union, alongside Philippe Trétiack, one of its star reporters. Their brief: to survey the fashions of a society that perestroika, the reforms Mikhail Gorbachev had launched two years earlier, was only beginning to loosen. On arrival, her belongings were searched. No matter. With a film Nikon slung over her shoulder, agnès b. set off through the city on her own account.

The Berlin Wall would fall two years later; the Soviet Union would dissolve in 1991. What held her attention, though, was neither ideology nor Stalinist architecture, but ordinary men and women whose gaze she caught on the street, sometimes lost in thought, always achingly human. There is no condescension in these pictures, made on the eve of the Soviet unraveling, only attention and curiosity.

Her eye settles on the rides of a fairground: a blonde girl grips the wheel of a rocket-shaped carousel car with the poise of a pilot. In a park, a woman braids the long hair of a child in a red dress, a scene spread across several successive frames, almost cinematic. At the animal market, what stops her is a man in a tweed jacket holding a Siamese cat against his chest. In the next frame, he is looking away. Just beside him, a hand tilts toward the light a cluster of glass flasks in which small red and black fish drift.

Color is everywhere, red above all. Was it the look of the moment, or was the photographer’s eye reaching instinctively for the emblematic shade? A woman and two little girls, all three in red sweaters, that color again, walk away toward a carousel. Elsewhere, a bride in a tulle veil smiles in front of the chrome grille of a black limousine topped with two interlocking rings, most likely a GAZ Chaika, the official sedan Soviet citizens could rent for a wedding.

A few souvenirs hang alongside the prints: a blue gymnastics leotard with white stripes, which reminded her of the one worn by Nadia Comăneci, the Romanian star of the 1976 Olympics. And, in the manner of the trinkets we all bring home from a trip, a small bust of Lenin in light metal, barely a foot tall. Relics of an era and a country so distant, and suddenly so close.

“5 jours à Moscou,” Maison agnès b., 17 rue Dieu, Paris 10e. Free admission, Monday to Friday 10 a.m.–7 p.m., Saturday 1–6 p.m. Through November 13, 2026, as part of Photo Days .

All photographs © agnès b., “5 jours à Moscou en 1987,” courtesy galerie du jour agnès b.
excerpt_original: Alongside an assignment for Elle, the designer photographed the Soviet Union at eye level: less the country than the people in it, caught on the street with curiosity and tenderness. These near-unseen pictures are now on view as part of Photo Days. L’article agnès b. in the Land…

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "安妮卡·伊丽莎白·冯·豪斯沃尔夫是北欧地区的开创性艺术家，其作品曾在欧洲和美国广泛展出。她以精心布景的影像闻名，这些作品通常具有纪实性的视觉表现力，且有多个系列曾从犯罪现场摄影中汲取灵感。冯·豪斯沃尔夫作品中的常青主题包括父权结构、犯罪学、全球资本主义、潜意识，以及对摄影图像本身的深厚兴趣。她的创作实践也延伸到了从模拟摄影到数字摄影的过渡，探讨摄影媒介的本质与条件。", "近年来，她的作品越来越基於现有的照片，主要取材自新闻和警察档案。这场新展览几乎全部采用了现成摄影和档案材料，这也是这位艺术家如今首选的工作方式。从她早期那些由她亲自拍摄、经过精心摆布的影像转变为此，根源于她对图像世界和图像本身的兴趣日益浓厚，而非对现实本身的关注。或许，从拍摄照片转向处理他人制作的照片，并没有那么大的偏离，因为她早期的作品同样更多地关注图像，而不是某个特定的“现实”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "冯·豪斯沃尔夫甚至用弗兰肯斯坦的实验室来形容她对他人图像的使用：拼凑碎片并对现有照片进行干预，成了一种复苏的行为。此过程中的选择构成了她的艺术方法。与此同时，她作品的标题也构成了被修改的图像及其新身份的重要方面。", "translated": true}, {"type": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这批新作品中也出现了德国牧羊犬，这是冯·豪斯沃尔夫自1990年代初以来创作实践中的一个关键母题。这种犬种——备受执法人员、民兵和罪犯的青睐，因此同样兼具威胁与保护的色彩——堪称完美的无声见证者：这位陪伴者目睹并听闻一切，却注定保持沉默。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "安妮卡·伊丽莎白·冯·豪斯沃尔夫于1967年出生，曾在斯德哥尔摩的瑞典皇家美术学院以及瑞典国立艺术、工艺与设计大学求学，自1994年起由安德烈恩-希普琴科画廊代理。她于1999年代表瑞典参加威尼斯双年展，其作品曾是三场重大中期回顾展的主题：2008年在斯德哥尔摩Magasin III举办的《Ich bin die Ecke aller Räume》；2016年在哥德堡哈苏基金会举办的《Grand Theory Hotel》；以及2021年至2022年在斯德哥尔摩和马尔默的瑞典国立博物馆（Moderna Museet）举办的《Alternative Secrecy》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "几十年来，安妮卡·伊丽莎白·冯·豪斯沃尔夫一直与法国艺术界保持着紧密的联系。她的作品曾在东京宫作为群展《L’autre sommeil》（1999–2000）的一部分展出，也曾在巴黎瑞典研究所（2016–2017）以及阿尔勒国际摄影节（2023）展出。她还将参加2026年10月10日至2027年1月3日在敦刻尔克大区当代艺术基金会（FRAC Grand Large）举办的展览《Je rêvais article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Andréhn-Schiptjenko Paris presents A Song for Europe , Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff ’s second solo exhibition with the Paris gallery. The opening will take place in the presence of the artist on Saturday 17 October, from 6pm to 9pm. The exhibition runs through 21 November 2026."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff is a seminal artist in the Nordic region and has been widely exhibited throughout Europe and the United States. She is well known for her carefully arranged images, often characterised by a documentary visual expression, and several of her series have drawn inspiration from crime scene photography. Recurring themes in von Hausswolff’s work include patriarchal structures, criminology, global capitalism, the subconscious, and a deep interest in the photographic image itself. Her practice also extends to the transition from analogue to digital photography, examining the nature and conditions of the photographic medium."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In recent years, her works have increasingly been based on existing photographs, drawing primarily on material sourced from press and police archives. This new exhibition makes almost exclusive use of found photography and archival material, the artist’s preferred mode of working today. The shift from her earlier, carefully staged images—which she photographed herself—is rooted in her growing interest in the world of images and the image per se, rather than in reality itself. Perhaps this step from taking photographs to working with those made by others is not such a significant departure, given that her earlier work was likewise more concerned with the image than with a particular “reality”."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Von Hausswolff even describes her use of others’ images in terms of Frankenstein’s laboratory: assembling fragments and intervening in existing photographs becomes an act of resuscitation. The choices made in this process constitute the artistic method. In parallel, the titles of her works form an important aspect of the altered image and its new identity."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Working solely with physical images—found in archives or purchased online or at flea markets—the material quality of the photographs is paramount. This physicality also translates into the images of analogue telephones, first seen in her work at the Hasselblad Foundation’s mid-career retrospective in 2016. The ergonomically designed receiver, held in the hand, establishes a bodily connection via the wire, coiled almost like an umbilical cord. Communication, in turn, necessitates remaining more or less in place, close to the telephone."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Also present in this new body of work is the German shepherd, a key trope in von Hausswolff’s practice since the early 1990s. The breed—preferred by law enforcement, militias, and criminals alike, and thus equally associated with threat and protection—is the silent witness par excellence: the companion who sees and hears everything, yet is bound to silence."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Born in 1967 and educated at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts and the University College of Arts, Crafts and Design in Stockholm, Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff has been represented by Andréhn-Schiptjenko since 1994. She represented Sweden at the Venice Biennale in 1999, and her work has been the subject of three major mid-career retrospectives: Ich bin die Ecke aller Räume at Magasin III, Stockholm (2008); Grand Theory Hotel at the Hasselblad Foundation, Gothenburg (2016); and Alternative Secrecy at Moderna Museet, Stockholm and Malmö (2021–2022)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff has maintained close ties with the French art scene for several decades. Her work has been presented at the Palais de Tokyo as part of L’autre sommeil (1999–2000), at the Swedish Institute in Paris (2016–2017), and at the Rencontres d’Arles (2023). She will also take part in the exhibition Je rêvais d’un autre monde at FRAC Grand Large, from 10 October 2026 to 3 January 2027."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Past institutional solo exhibitions include ARoS Kunstmuseum, Aarhus, Denmark; Magasin III, Stockholm, Sweden; La Conservera, Murcia, Spain; and Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen, Denmark. article_text:
Andréhn-Schiptjenko Paris presents A Song for Europe , Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff ’s second solo exhibition with the Paris gallery. The opening will take place in the presence of the artist on Saturday 17 October, from 6pm to 9pm. The exhibition runs through 21 November 2026.

Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff is a seminal artist in the Nordic region and has been widely exhibited throughout Europe and the United States. She is well known for her carefully arranged images, often characterised by a documentary visual expression, and several of her series have drawn inspiration from crime scene photography. Recurring themes in von Hausswolff’s work include patriarchal structures, criminology, global capitalism, the subconscious, and a deep interest in the photographic image itself. Her practice also extends to the transition from analogue to digital photography, examining the nature and conditions of the photographic medium.

In recent years, her works have increasingly been based on existing photographs, drawing primarily on material sourced from press and police archives. This new exhibition makes almost exclusive use of found photography and archival material, the artist’s preferred mode of working today. The shift from her earlier, carefully staged images—which she photographed herself—is rooted in her growing interest in the world of images and the image per se, rather than in reality itself. Perhaps this step from taking photographs to working with those made by others is not such a significant departure, given that her earlier work was likewise more concerned with the image than with a particular “reality”.

Von Hausswolff even describes her use of others’ images in terms of Frankenstein’s laboratory: assembling fragments and intervening in existing photographs becomes an act of resuscitation. The choices made in this process constitute the artistic method. In parallel, the titles of her works form an important aspect of the altered image and its new identity.

Working solely with physical images—found in archives or purchased online or at flea markets—the material quality of the photographs is paramount. This physicality also translates into the images of analogue telephones, first seen in her work at the Hasselblad Foundation’s mid-career retrospective in 2016. The ergonomically designed receiver, held in the hand, establishes a bodily connection via the wire, coiled almost like an umbilical cord. Communication, in turn, necessitates remaining more or less in place, close to the telephone.

Also present in this new body of work is the German shepherd, a key trope in von Hausswolff’s practice since the early 1990s. The breed—preferred by law enforcement, militias, and criminals alike, and thus equally associated with threat and protection—is the silent witness par excellence: the companion who sees and hears everything, yet is bound to silence.

Born in 1967 and educated at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts and the University College of Arts, Crafts and Design in Stockholm, Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff has been represented by Andréhn-Schiptjenko since 1994. She represented Sweden at the Venice Biennale in 1999, and her work has been the subject of three major mid-career retrospectives: Ich bin die Ecke aller Räume at Magasin III, Stockholm (2008); Grand Theory Hotel at the Hasselblad Foundation, Gothenburg (2016); and Alternative Secrecy at Moderna Museet, Stockholm and Malmö (2021–2022).

Annika Elisabeth von Hausswolff has maintained close ties with the French art scene for several decades. Her work has been presented at the Palais de Tokyo as part of L’autre sommeil (1999–2000), at the Swedish Institute in Paris (2016–2017), and at the Rencontres d’Arles (2023). She will also take part in the exhibition Je rêvais d’un autre monde at FRAC Grand Large, from 10 October 2026 to 3 January 2027.

Past institutional solo exhibitions include ARoS Kunstmuseum, Aarhus, Denmark; Magasin III, Stockholm, Sweden; La Conservera, Murcia, Spain; and Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen, Denmark. Her work is represented in the collections of Fotomuseum Winterthur, KIASMA, Helsinki, SFMOMA, San Francisco, MCA Chicago, Moderna Museet, Stockholm, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, among others.

Her work is also held in the collections of the Astrup Fearnley Collection, Museet for Moderne Kunst, Oslo, Norway; Fonds National d’Art Contemporain, Paris, France; Fotomuseum Winterthur, Switzerland; FRAC Languedoc–Roussillon, Montpellier, France; FRAC Nord–Pas-de-Calais, France; Göteborgs Konstmuseum, Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard University Art Museums, Cambridge, USA; Hasselblad Center, Gothenburg, Sweden; KIASMA, Helsinki, Finland; Länsmuseet Gävleborg, Gävle, Sweden; the National Museum of Women in the Arts, New York, USA; the National Gallery of Denmark, Copenhagen, Denmark; and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, USA.

article_text:
F ifty years ago this December, cinema’s greatest underdog story hit the screen, a tale about a Philadelphia ham-and-egger who takes the world heavyweight boxing champ all the way to the final bell, losing the fight on a judge’s decision but winning the hearts of a nation. That film, of course, was Rocky. Its creation, famously, was no less remarkable an underdog story – one about an out-of-work character actor with the curious name of Sylvester Stallone who wrote his own boxing movie then managed to convince a studio not only to finance it, but also to cast him in the title role. He then went one further than the character he was playing by earning the top prize: a best picture Oscar.

If you thought, half a century on, Rocky’s punching power – its unerring ability to make heroes out of zeroes – has faded, think again. This, after all, is a movie franchise whose stirring qualities are enough to make thousands of people hurtle up all 72 of the Philadelphia Museum of Art’s steps every year in homage to its plucky pugilist .

And now Rocky has birthed a third great underdog story. This one is about a 27-year-old New Yorker who, through grit, persistence and a never-ending stream of unsolicited audition tapes, bags the role of a lifetime and propels himself into the Oscar running, alongside the likes of Tom Cruise, Matt Damon and John Malkovich. His name is Anthony Ippolito and he’s playing Sly Stallone himself in Peter Farrelly’s rousing, making-of movie I Play Rocky .

The role, which follows Stallone from his early struggles in New York to movie greatness in LA, is one Ippolito has been circling – like Ali or Tyson rounding their prey – for years, before the project even had a script. Such was his desperation to play Stallone, he started sending in self-taped performances of what he thought those making the film might be after, an experience that felt like “sending your work into the abyss – even more so when no one’s asking for your audition in the first place”.

It’s a process, Ippolito remembers with a wry smile, that could feel “a little discouraging”, particularly when film websites were tipping big names for the role – Superman David Corenswet, Jacob Elordi, even Timothée Chalamet. Ippolito recalls: “People around me said, ‘Don’t get your hopes up, they’re probably looking at bigger names. That’s Hollywood.’”

He would not be deterred, though, and his self-confidence was justified: according to Farrelly, Ippolito was the first person he and the film’s producers looked at for the part. And once they saw him there was no point in auditioning anyone else.

Speaking to Ippolito by video call from a hotel room in Rome, it’s not easy to discern immediately what made those producers so convinced of his Sly-ness. Granted, he doesn’t look dissimilar to Rocky-era Stallone – the square jaw and mop of dark hair are present and correct – but his features are softer, more boyband, and his voice is noticeably higher than Stallone’s bassy drawl. You’d be more likely to compare him to a young Al Pacino – fitting, as Ippolito played Pacino in another making-of project, The Offer , a TV series about the protracted creation of The Godfather.

Yet the moment the opening credits of I Play Rocky roll, a remarkable transformation occurs. Ippolito’s voice drops an octave, and he affects that stuffy sinus-heavy delivery of Stallone’s. His eyes droop, his chin juts, his shoulders seem to grow rounder and he starts to move in that loping shuffle. He looks broader and more imposing, too – the result, Ippolito says, of a bulking-up regime that involved “a lot of eating, a lot of protein … it required an entire lifestyle shift”.

It’s a performance that could so easily lapse into lazy caricature – or even worse, punching down, given that Stallone’s drooping features and slurred speech are the result of forceps injury at birth. But Ippolito is so note perfect that even Stallone has been in touch to offer his approval. “He had a positive reaction and I’m very grateful – because this is, in a lot of ways, a love letter to what he persevered through.”

The film, Ippolito says, covers a “very dark, lonely time” in Stallone’s life, when he worked in a fishmonger’s and appeared in an adult movie to scrape together rent. What serious roles he did get tended to be bit parts as tough guys, cops or thugs. He was routinely belittled for his speech and looks – particularly by his domineering father, played by Matt Dillon in the film. But Stallone had a remarkable raw talent hidden under the surface. “There’s this incongruence,” Ippolito says. “People would mistake him for being, um, maybe not smart – just a strong, burly guy with this slur. And then he’s actually a brilliant writer. Burt Young [his Rocky co-star] called him ‘an orphan in life’ with ‘a big fire burning and no place to put it’. You can feel this great depth and intensity.”

I Play Rocky doesn’t seem terribly preoccupied with these roiling internal dynamics – though that isn’t to its detriment. It’s not hard to see why crowds have chimed with the film, which turns Stallone’s story into part inspirational sports movie, part comedy caper. Farrelly has great fun in depicting the scrappy, seat-of-its-pants production of the original film, which couldn’t go a day over for risk of its studio shutting the whole thing down: scenes are rattled off in single, frenzied takes; Stallone limps through filming with a strained leg tendon, then a broken hand from punching a frozen side of beef in the film’s famous meat-locker scene; at one point, cast and crew have to squeeze into a walk-in freezer with their equipment to hide from a union rep threatening to take their filming permit away.

The most entertaining section, though, comes before Rocky has even been greenlit, when the film’s producers are trying desperately to convince Stallone to give up the title role in return for a life-changing sum of money. No matter how many zeroes are added, Sly stands firm: no starring role, no deal. This despite him having few career prospects and a heavily pregnant wife. It’s a remarkable act of brinkmanship – at one point, Stallone is forced to sell his own dog to make ends meet – but it proves successful.

after newsletter promotion

Stallone turned down $300,000, the equivalent of almost $2m today. Would Ippolito have gone to such extremes? “I don’t know, it’s a lot of money,” he laughs “I don’t want to make myself sound spineless! But it’s certainly tempting. I guess that’s what makes it so incredible, maddening almost. I think there’s a certain naive quality. Like he was able to just, at a young age, almost not know the rules so he could break them.”

In another life, rather than playing an actor playing a boxer, Ippolito might have been a baseball player. At three years old, he was a pitching prodigy able to throw a ball at “40 miles per hour or something”, a talent that led him to appear on an episode of Ripley’s Believe it or Not!. For much of his childhood, playing baseball professionally was “the main goal”, and he carried on at a high level at college. “I learned a lot about acting inadvertently,” he says, “because there’s a ton of failure in that sport.”

By his late teens, he had started to take acting seriously. He began picking up walk-on parts in films: David Chase’s coming of age movie Not Fade Away, where he got to watch James Gandolfini from afar; Julianne Moore comedy-drama The English Teacher; and Adam Sandler vehicle Pixels, where he first understood the appeal of doing this thing full-time. “I was like, ‘Wow, these guys look like they’re really having fun at work.’ That stuck out.”

After college, his career moved up a gear: there was a main role in edgy Netflix high-school drama Grand Army , then his appearance as Pacino in The Offer. How does it feel to play not one but two of the most famous actors alive? “It’ll throw you, for sure. But it’s also an incredible opportunity to explore stuff. There’s almost a voyeuristic quality to it – like an infinity staircase.”

Now, with the success of I Play Rocky, Ippolito is finding himself among the big names, rather than impersonating them. He recently met Andrew Garfield and “is still recovering”. More encounters will surely come in awards season: his Stallone performance is being talked up for a best actor nomination, which would put him up against “people I’ve looked up to for the last 20 years”. Don’t count Anthony Ippolito out yet.

editorial_title_zh: 时尚界人士毁了伦敦弗里兹艺博会的体验吗？

article_text:
Frieze Week has become a pilgrimage site for fashion folk. Since 2022, the fashion population has been aggressively migrating to the art fair; that same year McQueen and Roksanda staged their runways shows to coincide with Frieze London and Frieze Masters. In the lead-up to Frieze Week, there has been some chatter among art journalists, publicists and gallerists about the increasing number of fashion attendees making a pitstop just for an Instagram photo.

So, has fashion ruined Frieze?

“Ruined might be a stretch, but I do think that the glut of selfie-hungry fashion girlies may have somewhat cheapened the experience, and I say that as a selfie-hungry fashion girlie myself,” Mahoro Seward, fashion and style editor at British Vogue , told ARTnews .

The Wednesday VIP day has become a day of who’s who: This year’s attendees included Tilda Swinton, Raf Simons, Dries Van Noten, Monica Barbaro, and Bianca Jagger wearing John Galliano’s Zara collection. And the outfits at the fair, or costumes for lack of a better word, got more conceptual (perhaps even more so than the artwork). There were leather, fur, sequins, and two people in matching PVC catsuits in action inside the hot tent.

During London Fashion Week such kooky outfits grant cheers from street style photographers, but at Frieze, they’re side-eyed. “In fashion, the more shameless you are, the more you get praised. Fashion people have made a gimmick of the fashion industry,” said one fashion editor, who asked to remain anonymous. That’s not to say that art folk don’t like dressing up and expressing themselves, but it’s usually in a pleated Issey Miyake piece or a neat Hermès overcoat or Evelyne bag.

Kristell Chadé, Frieze’s executive director of fairs, is of a “the more, the merrier” opinion. It’s economically beneficial for Frieze and the galleries when fashion wants to get involved, she says. In 2023, Stone Island joined Frieze London as a partner and offered bursaries to 34 emerging galleries, while Dunhill launched its inaugural partnership with Frieze Masters. “Frieze is a platform for various voices and different disciplines. I think having that richness and diversity is what makes the fair unique,” Chadé told ARTnews .

More brands have started to take note. Tiffany & Co. has been a partner for Frieze’s Artist-to-Artist initiative since last year and similarly; Loewe has sponsored Frieze London’s VIP program. (It also doesn’t hurt that Loewe’s campaigns make for beautiful imagery on the back of the fair map brochure.)

“Then again,” Seward, the British Vogue editor, said, “I don’t think Frieze is exactly hallowed ground. Yes, there’s brilliant work on show of critical merit, but it’s fundamentally a commercial forum.”

Fashion’s invasion of the art world is a strategic ploy—brands are trying to lure the same consumers that are splashing out more than $6 million on Jan Brueghel the Elder’s Still Life of Flowers in a Stoneware Vase (1607–8), which sold for that amount at Hauser & Wirth’s Frieze Masters booth. The luxury fashion industry is grappling its own slowdown: Consumers are spending cautiously, and brands are increasingly raising their prices. It’s the reason fashion has inhabited spaces such as F1, the US Open and Frieze London.

When Roksanda Ilinčić staged her spring 2023 show the night before Frieze London commenced, she did so because her audience is “much more art and creatives-related, which is incredible because it’s a big portion of my customers and usually they’re not able to come to the show, but now they’re all in town (for Frieze), so it’s lovely to be able to see them,” she told me at the time .

“Fashion loves to get its hands on everything. We’ve seen it in sports, art, theater and Hollywood. Fashion is its own force,” Sunita Kumar Nair, author of Ace: The Times & Style of Tennis , told ARTnews . In her book, she observes how fashion has become a Trojan horse in tennis and can see the same pattern taking form in the art world. “Fashion is like a form of nature: It can either destroy or create if it’s in excess. For me, writing about tennis and fashion was just a really inevitable angle that I saw because of its popularity.”

Shifting the blame onto fashion folk for ruining the Frieze experience may be unfair, but a quick scan of Instagram, they are always the first to plant their flag. “Posting from Frieze is the new ‘I was here’ scratched on a wall,” said one veteran fashion publicist. After all, swanning around in Balenciaga and air kissing with a tulip of Ruinart in hand has never been a crime. Not yet, anyway.
excerpt_original: Since 2022, the fashion population has been aggressively migrating to the art fair in their kooky garments.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 介于神童话与社会纪实之间，《爱尔兰旅行者》（Irish Travellers，将于10月28日上映）点亮了我们的秋天。影片导演、法爱混血的亚历山大·墨菲（Alexander Murphy）在片中讲述了一个爱尔兰旅行者家庭的日常生活。他流利的法语和语速……

"我跟奥赖利一家相处的时间越多，就越喜欢他们，也就越想在没有镜头的情况下见到他们。拍摄几乎成了次要的。孩子们非常迷人，母亲有着女超人的一面，而父亲帕（Pa’）几乎就像是一个小说中的人物。某种粗犷与某种温柔结合在一个水牛般的身躯里，我觉得这很雄伟。他是一个从不表达自己感受的人。但他有走神的时候，那时所有的情绪都会倾泻而出。只要架起摄像机，就能拍到绝妙的东西。我完全改变了对这部电影的构思方式，并在2024年决定和他们一起完成它。", "从一开始，他们就同意让我拍摄，因为我每次去都会带回影像。和他们一起看这些影像是一段有趣的时光。然而，尽管在拖车前和孩子们一起拍摄很容易，但被邀请进内部去谈论私密的事情则是另一回事。起初，我是一个奇怪的、有异国情调的人物，闯入了他们的世界。我告诉自己，必须花时间与他们相处，直到他们最终对我感到厌烦。我想既成为布景的一部分，又成为这个充满爱意、让我有点嫉妒的家庭的一部分。在捕捉东西之前建立联系对我很重要。渐渐地，摄像机成了这个家庭的延伸，某种意义上的第十一个孩子。但是，要在镜头前捕捉到一句“我爱你”，花了我五年的工作。", Plard），他成功地与这个家庭建立了非常深厚的联系。他的工作仅限于此，所以我依然独自负责画面和声音。但过了一会儿，我熟悉了这个家庭的编舞、他们小空间的节奏，我喜欢让摄像机长时间运转。开场镜头就是这样拍出来的[注：固定镜头拍摄于拖车入口前，孩子们和父母进进出出]：我看着这段芭蕾重复上演，有一天早晨我决定把机器架在那里十五分钟。", "translated": true}, {"type": "我想展示爱尔兰的四季，但诚然，这些夏天的小片段是我年轻时和表兄弟们一起经历过的。在河里游泳、在加油站买意大利冰淇淋、在麦田里奔跑，这就是我的童年。一开始，我的灵感来源是安德烈·阿诺德（Andrea Arnold）或肯·洛奇（Ken Loach）的作品，后来我放弃了这些，转而专注于我的叔叔们拍摄的家庭录像，以及约瑟夫·寇德卡（Josef Koudelka）的摄影作品。他在1970年代在斯洛伐克、斯洛文尼亚和法国拍摄过一组非凡的吉普赛人系列。那些黑白影像极为惊艳，他捕捉到了人们的能量与美感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "这个问题一直伴随着我的整个拍摄过程。我尽量不掩饰奥赖利一家的真实面貌，包括他们做出在我们看来难以理解的决定时，比如当父母拒绝了一套分配给他们的房屋。我们的目的不是去神化他们，而是保持诚实。这是一个在爱尔兰备受污名化的族群，在人们对他们缺乏了解的同时，却引发了一种莫名的仇恨。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": C’était une évidence, j’étais fasciné par cette arène cinématographique. Une fois parti à leur rencontre, je me suis rapidement rendu compte que cela allait me prendre un temps phénoménal. article_text:
Comment avez-vous rencontré la famille O’Reilly au cœur de ce documentaire ?

Quand j’ai commencé dans ce métier, je me suis dit que j’allais forcément faire un jour un film sur les voyageurs. C’était une évidence, j’étais fasciné par cette arène cinématographique. Une fois parti à leur rencontre, je me suis rapidement rendu compte que cela allait me prendre un temps phénoménal. J’ai vu plein de communautés, plein de familles qui m’ont touché, dont les O’Reilly pour la première fois en 2020. Quand je les ai rencontrés, je m’attendais à des gens libres et extrêmement fiers. En réalité, j’ai vu des individus asphyxiés par cette société irlandaise qui les cloisonne et les pousse soit à se sédentariser dans des endroits précis, soit à s’installer dans des maisons ou des appartements, allant à l’encontre de leur façon de vivre. Il y a un taux de dépression énorme et sept fois plus de suicides chez les voyageurs que dans l’ensemble de la population irlandaise.

Qu’est-ce qui vous a poussé vers un film intime plutôt qu’un portrait d’une communauté entière ?

Plus je passais du temps avec les O’Reilly, plus je les aimais et plus j’avais envie de les voir sans caméra. Le tournage était devenu presque secondaire. Les enfants sont somptueux, la mère a un côté superwoman et Pa’, le père, est presque un personnage de fiction. Il y a une certaine brutalité et une forme de tendresse unies dans un corps de buffle que je trouve majestueux. C’est quelqu’un qui n’exprime jamais ce qu’il ressent. Mais il a des moments d’absence durant lesquels toutes les émotions dégoulinent. Il n’y avait qu’à poser sa caméra pour avoir quelque chose de sublime. J’ai complètement changé ma façon de penser le film et en 2024, j’ai décidé de le faire avec eux.

A-t-il été facile de les convaincre ?

Dès le début, ils ont accepté que je les filme car je revenais toujours avec des images la fois suivante. C’était un moment amusant de les regarder ensemble. Mais autant il est facile de tourner devant la caravane avec les enfants, autant être invité à l’intérieur pour parler de choses intimes, c’est un autre délire. Au départ, j’étais un personnage étrange, exotique, qui rentrait dans leur monde. Je me suis dis qu’il fallait passer du temps avec eux pour qu’ils finissent par s’ennuyer de moi. Je voulais faire partie à la fois du décor et de cette famille débordante d’amour, que je jalousais un peu. Cela a été très important pour moi de créer un lien avant de capter des choses. Au fur et à mesure, la caméra est devenue une extension de cette famille, leur onzième enfant en quelque sorte. Mais pour capter un “je t’aime” devant la caméra, il a fallu cinq ans de travail.

Quel dispositif avez-vous utilisé pour vous approcher d’eux au plus près ?

J’ai commencé seul avec un appareil photo. À un moment, j’ai tenté de faire venir un ingénieur du son et cela a été une catastrophe. Un intrus dans le cocon protégé des O’Reilly, cela obligeait à repartir de zéro. Mais comme cela restait un peu lourd seul, j’ai fait venir Jean-Baptiste Plard, mon co-scénariste, qui a réussi à construire un lien très fort avec la famille. Son travail était uniquement celui-ci, donc j’étais toujours seul à l’image et au son. Mais au bout d’un moment, je connaissais la chorégraphie de cette famille, le rythme de son petit espace, et j’aimais bien laisser la caméra tourner longtemps. C’est ce qui s’est produit pour la séquence d’ouverture [filmée devant l’entrée de la caravane en plan fixe pendant que les enfants et les parents entrent et sortent, ndlr] : j’ai vu ce ballet se répéter et j’ai décidé un matin de me poser quinze minutes.

Comment avez-vous construit l’identité esthétique du film, très reconnaissable notamment par ses tons chauds qui tranchent avec l’image un peu pluvieuse et grise que l’on peut avoir de l’Irlande ?

Je voulais montrer toutes les saisons de l’Irlande mais c’est vrai que ces morceaux d’été, c’est ce que j’ai vécu plus jeune avec mes cousins. La baignade dans la rivière, la glace à l’italienne à la station-service, courir dans les champs de blé, c’est mon enfance. J’avais comme référence au départ les œuvres d’Andrea Arnold ou Ken Loach, avant de les abandonner pour me concentrer sur les films de famille tournés par mes oncles, ainsi que les photographies de Josef Koudelka. Il a fait une série extraordinaire sur des gitans en Slovaquie, en Slovénie et en France dans les années 1970. Ce sont des clichés en noir et blanc extraordinaires, il a chopé l’énergie et la beauté des gens.

Vous rythmez le film de scènes similaires dans lesquelles le père, et parfois les enfants, grimpent sur un sulky attelé à leurs chevaux et s’en vont trotter sur la route. Quel est leur rôle ?

Pour Pa’, le sulky représente une façon de s’échapper. Il y a quelque chose de thérapeutique dans le fait de retrouver une certaine sensation de liberté. Mine de rien, celle-ci est menacée, avec les voitures qui passent et klaxonnent. Cela vient rappeler que les voyageurs gênent et ne sont jamais totalement libres.

Aux deux-tiers du film, Pa’ est condamné à de la prison. Pourquoi avoir choisi de passer sous silence la raison de sa condamnation ?

C’était un pacte passé avec la famille. J’avais la responsabilité de ne pas tout dévoiler, je ne voulais pas que cela devienne voyeuriste et je pense que de toute façon, ce n’est pas essentiel pour comprendre le film. Surtout, j’ai commencé ce projet par le prisme des enfants, et même du conte, car il y a quelque chose de féérique dans cette vie coupée du monde. Or, les enfants sentent bien les tensions mais ne comprennent pas tous les tenants et les aboutissants.

Comment avez-vous veillé à garder la bonne distance avec votre sujet pour ne tomber ni dans l’angélisme, ni dans le misérabilisme ?

C’est un questionnement qui m’a poursuivi pendant tout le tournage. J’ai essayé de ne pas cacher qui sont les O’Reilly, y compris leurs décisions qui nous paraissent incompréhensibles, comme lorsque les parents refusent une maison qui leur est proposée. Le but n’était pas de les magnifier mais d’être honnête. C’est un peuple très stigmatisé en Irlande, qui suscite une forme de haine alors qu’il est méconnu.

Les O’Reilly ont-ils vu le film ?

Nous leur avons organisé une projection au cinéma. Ils n’y étaient jamais allés de leur vie, on a fait la totale, avec les pop corn et tout. J’ai senti qu’ils avaient un peu peur avant. Après, ils ne m’ont jamais dit s’ils avaient aimé ou pas mais j’ai quand même décelé de la fierté et de la reconnaissance. Je crois qu’ils se sont trouvés beaux.

translated_title_zh: 亚历山大·默菲(Alexander Murphy):在摄像机前拍摄“我爱你”需要五年的工作
translated_excerpt_zh: 在童话故事和社交见证之间的一半路,“爱尔兰旅行者”(10月28日)照亮了我们的秋天,其导演,法国爱尔兰人亚历山大·默菲,讲述了一个爱尔兰旅行者的家庭的日常。

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : OneTwoThree Media is launching worldwide sales ahead of the AFM on the sci-fi feature Life 2.0 , written and directed by Star Trek alum Michael Dorn ( Star Trek: The Next Generation, Star Trek: Deep Space Nine ), who also stars.

Dorn is joined in the film by fellow Star Trek franchise vets Marina Sirtis ( Star Trek: The Next Generation ), Michelle Hurd ( Star Trek: Picard ) and Dominic Keating ( Star Trek: Enterprise ).

Related Stories

Renée Zellweger, Dominic Sessa & Peter Dinklage Set For Sacha Gervasi’s High Concept Comedy Drama ‘Darlington’ – AFM

William Shatner Remembers ‘Star Trek’ Co-Star Walter Koenig

Dorn “plays an operative in deep-space isolation, with only an AI hologram for company, until an enigmatic new companion arrives. An accident uncovers the truth about their origins, forcing a fight for survival against motives engineered back on Earth.”

Produced by Emily Corcoran for Cork Films and Michael Dorn for Sabrejet, the film was shot entirely in the UK. The project marks Dorn’s feature directing debut and is the first science-fiction feature to reunite Dorn and Sirtis since 2002’s Star Trek: Nemesis .

Watch on Deadline

Alongside this title, the company has taken on international sales for two further features: the UK sci-fi comedy Time Travel Is Dangerous! and U.S. psychological thriller The Black Box .

Also new to OneTwoThree Media’s slate is Time Travel Is Dangerous!, directed by Chris Reading. The London-set comedy feature is narrated by Stephen Fry and stars Johnny Vegas, Jane Horrocks, Sophie Thompson and Mark Heap, with Brian Blessed voicing an octopus monster. It premiered at the Austin Film Festival.

The third new addition is U.S. film The Black Box , described as a psychological thriller directed by Vitor Cardoso and Ricardo R. Marques. Set in the Hollywood Hills during a graduation farewell party, “a group of friends stumbles upon ‘The Black Box’ — an elusive internet sensation and twisted version of Truth or Dare said to choose its own players.”

Deals across the slate were negotiated for OneTwoThree Media by Joey Dawson with Emily Corcoran of Cork Films on Life 2.0 , and Chris Reading of The Unreason Ltd on Time Travel Is Dangerous! , and Alan Green with Mark Silba on The Black Box .

ロンドン・ウエストエンドやニューヨーク・ブロードウェイで大きな話題を呼んだ舞台「ジャイアント」を映像収録しスクリーン上映。「チャーリーとチョコレート工場」の原作小説などで知られるイギリスの児童文学作家ロアルド・ダールを主人公に、彼のキャリアを揺るがした実在のスキャンダルを描く。 1983年、イギリス。著名な児童文学作家ロアルド・ダールは、反ユダヤ主義的な内容の記事を書いたことで批判を浴びていた。ダールは自宅を訪ねてきた出版関係者たちを相手に、緊迫した会話を繰り広げる。 「教皇選挙」などの名優ジョン・リスゴーが実在の作家ロアルド・ダールを演じ、ウエストエンド公演でローレンス・オリビエ賞の最優秀主演男優賞、ブロードウェイ公演でトニー賞の主演男優賞（戯曲部門）に輝いた。20年以上にわたりイギリス演劇界で活躍してきた演出家マーク・ローゼンブラットが脚本を手がけ、初戯曲にしてローレンス・オリビエ賞の最優秀新作戯曲賞を受賞。「英国万歳！」「ミス・シェパードをお手本に」など映画監督としても知られる名演出家ニコラス・ハイトナーが演出を担った。

article_text:
The Bay Theater in Pacific Palisades will officially reopen on Friday, a month after it was announced that Paramount Pictures is taking over the cinemas.

Paramount Pictures, Caruso and The Lot have reimagined the theaters with cutting-edge cinema technology that includes “luxury seating, elevated dining and exceptional hospitality, while preserving the intimate neighborhood character that has made it a community favorite.”

Related Stories

'Kefi' Review: A Grief-Stricken Family Reunion Is Beset by Aliens, Drugs and Dinosaurs in Kisin Saito's Kaleidoscopic, Genre-Fluid Debut

Previously operated by Netflix, the theaters have been closed since the devastating wildfires in January 2025. The multiplex is located in Rick Caruso ’s Palisades Village shopping area, which reopened in August after extensive remediation and repairs due to the fires.

First-run films playing at the Bay include Johnny Depp’s “Ebenezer,” which opens nationwide Friday, as well as “The Cat in the Hat,” “Wild Horse Nine,” “You Can See Everything” and “Godzilla Minus Zero.”

Operated by luxury dine-in cinema company The Lot, the Bay offers five auditoriums with immersive surround sound and laser projection. Theaters include customizable seating with adjustable foot, back, head and neck rests, USB charging, personal dining tables with custom lighting and service buttons for food and beverage ordering.

The made-to-order menu, served directly to seats, includes appetizers, snacks, burgers, entrées and desserts, plus a premium beverage program with wine, beer, mocktails and signature cocktails including the Pacific Blush, Sunset Mule and Coastline Cantarito.

The lounge area and full-service bar feature a video wall for sports viewing, giving moviegoers a place to gather before and after films.

In addition to first-run films, the Bay will program nostalgic classics, curated screenings and special events.
